name: Combined hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma
lead: Which gate this patient is at when the diagnosis is still provisional, and which document will actually govern the transplant decision.
gatelabel: The decision in front of you

gates.name: 0 · Is this cHCC-CCA, and can imaging tell you?
crit: A liver mass whose enhancement carries both hepatocellular and non-hepatocellular features, or an LR-M observation in an at-risk liver
AFP and CA 19-9 both raised, or one raised against an enhancement pattern that does not match it
Imaging that reads LR-5 in a patient with no cirrhosis, no chronic hepatitis B and no prior HCC
A biopsy or specimen already reporting one component with features of the other
A tumour already resected or transplanted whose pathology reports both differentiations
gates.ask: Is this one tumour with two differentiations, and have I stopped expecting imaging to settle it?

standard.t: The diagnosis is histological. WHO 2019 requires unequivocal hepatocytic and cholangiocytic differentiation within a single tumour, made on routine haematoxylin and eosin, with immunostains supportive rather than essential.
standard.pref: Every case. The international consensus that fed the WHO fifth edition is explicit that diagnosis rests on routine histopathology and that immunostains are supportive, not essential — which matters because a tumour can be biphenotypic at the level of the individual cell rather than containing two separate areas. The fifth edition's own summary states the requirement the same way and lists what is now outside the category: the Allen double-cancer and combined types, and the Goodman collision and fibrolamellar types.
standard.avoid: Do not make this diagnosis on imaging, on tumour markers, or on an immunohistochemical panel alone. NCCN states plainly that diagnosis through imaging is difficult because the features are a mixture of both, that misdiagnosis may occur, and that thorough pathology review is recommended where cHCC-CCA is suspected.
standard.note: WHO 2019 dropped the stem-cell subtypes of the 2010 classification and reassigned cholangiolocarcinoma, formerly the cholangiolocellular subtype, to small-duct intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma unless an unequivocal HCC component coexists. It keeps the classical type and recognises intermediate cell carcinoma as a named subtype. Downgraded from B to C on the full-text read for two reasons the documents themselves supply: the 2018 consensus carries no evidence grading and set no threshold for how much of each component is required, and when the resulting definition is applied in practice pathologist agreement with the reference cHCC-CCA diagnosis was kappa 0.19, with inter-observer agreement kappa 0.37, across 405 cases. The definition is the right one to use; it is not a reproducible measurement. See the quick reference for what moved where.

standard.t: Treat an LR-M read as a reason to get tissue, not as a diagnosis — LR-M means definite or probable malignancy not specific for HCC, and it is a category that deliberately gives up specificity for the mixed tumour.
standard.pref: Any at-risk patient whose observation is categorised LR-M, and any patient in whom one LR-M feature appears alongside otherwise HCC-like enhancement. On gadoxetate-enhanced MRI in 33 cHCC-CCA against 66 HCC, at least one LR-M feature was present in 93.9% of cHCC-CCA but also in 51.5% of HCC, so specificity was 48.5%. Note that the same paper reports the HCC figure as 48.5% in one place and 51.5% in another; both cannot be right and the direction of the finding — that half of true HCC carries an LR-M feature — is unaffected.
standard.avoid: Do not read LR-M as 'this is cHCC-CCA', and do not read its absence as exclusion. Requiring three or more LR-M features raises accuracy to 80.8% but drops sensitivity to 54.5%, so that rule misses nearly half of these tumours. And targetoid appearance on its own is close to useless here: it was present in 75.8% of cHCC-CCA but also in 65.2% of the HCC controls. There is no threshold that both finds and confirms this tumour.
standard.note: The policy-relevant figure is the other way round. In 105 HCC and 73 non-HCC malignancies read at two transplant centres, LR-5 was 89–90% specific but only 55–66% sensitive for HCC, and cHCC-CCA made up 63–86% of the false-positive LR-5 reads; LR-M and LR-TIV together identified only 70.8% and 62.3% of cHCC-CCA against 88% and 92% of intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma. LI-RADS protects the HCC diagnosis and detects iCCA as non-HCC; it does not keep this tumour out of an imaging-based HCC pathway. Both case-control series down-sampled HCC relative to true prevalence, so only sensitivity and specificity transfer.

standard.t: Draw AFP and CA 19-9 together at baseline and record the date and the biliary and inflammatory state at which each was taken; a discrepancy between the markers and the enhancement pattern is itself the signal.
standard.pref: Every new liver mass in which cHCC-CCA is on the differential. In a 137-patient three-centre gadoxetate study separating 52 cHCC-CCA from 85 mass-forming iCCA, all in hepatitis B infection or HBV cirrhosis, AFP above 100 ng/mL was the only independent predictor of cHCC-CCA (OR 3.42, p=0.012); AFP was raised in 69.2% of cHCC-CCA against 31.8% of iCCA (p<0.001) while CA 19-9 was raised in 50.0% against 70.6% (p=0.019). AFP above 100 ng/mL alone gave an AUC of 0.687 (sensitivity 69.2%, specificity 68.2%); adding targetoid diffusion restriction raised it to 0.807 (sensitivity 88.5%, specificity 64.7%, Z=3.196, p=0.001).
standard.avoid: Do not expect dual marker elevation to make the diagnosis, and do not quote a single figure for how often it happens: the review literature puts simultaneous AFP and CA 19-9 elevation at about 15% and at about 20% of patients, while a 21-patient Japanese cohort using a wider definition — any HCC marker with any biliary marker — reported 57.1%. Do not use a normal AFP to exclude the diagnosis either: in the Japanese nationwide survey AFP was under 10 ng/mL in 46.2% and CA 19-9 under 37 U/mL in 60.0%, and NCCN notes AFP levels in cHCC-CCA do not differ significantly from those in HCC. A normal CA 19-9 is equally unhelpful — it was in the normal range in 57.9% of 19 transplant recipients whose explants showed cHCC-CCA.
standard.note: NCCN's Principles of Core Needle Biopsy lists raised CA 19-9 or CEA with suspicion of iCCA or cHCC-CCA as an indication for biopsy even when the lesion meets imaging criteria for HCC. That footnote is the practical trigger this gate turns on. What the marker work cannot do is the thing that matters most for a transplant pathway: the 137-patient study had no HCC comparator group at all, so it says nothing about the error of calling a cHCC-CCA an HCC and listing it.

opts.name: Gadoxetate-enhanced MRI, read against the LR-M feature set
opts.when: The most studied single test. Rim arterial phase hyperenhancement, peripheral washout, delayed central enhancement and targetoid diffusion restriction are the features that pull a tumour out of the HCC algorithm. Targetoid appearance alone was present in 75.8% of cHCC-CCA — but also in 65.2% of matched HCC, so by itself it separates almost nothing.
opts.pref: The at-risk patient with an indeterminate or targetoid mass where the question is whether to biopsy and whether to involve the transplant team before anyone does.
opts.avoid: Do not expect it to separate cHCC-CCA from iCCA. In the three-centre study of tumours with rim or progressive enhancement, progressive enhancement (OR 0.283, p=0.013), targetoid appearance on hepatobiliary phase (OR 0.196, p=0.001) and targetoid diffusion restriction (OR 0.157, p<0.001) all predicted iCCA rather than cHCC-CCA, and only raised AFP went the other way. The best combination still mislabels about a third of iCCA as cHCC-CCA, at 64.7% specificity.

opts.name: Contrast-enhanced ultrasound with tumour markers
opts.when: In 134 pathologically confirmed lesions including 35 cHCC-CCA, 74.3% of cHCC-CCA were assigned LR-M on contrast-enhanced ultrasound and the rest were not — 25.7% were assigned LR-5.
opts.pref: A problem-solving tool at a centre with the expertise, in a patient in whom MRI is contraindicated or non-diagnostic.
opts.avoid: Not for whole-liver assessment, surveillance or staging — NCCN does not recommend it for those. And read the performance figures, not the LR-M proportion: the CEUS LI-RADS criteria for cHCC-CCA were 40.0% sensitive and 89.9% specific with an AUC of 0.649, and the authors recalculated the positive predictive value at realistic disease prevalence as 1.6% to 39.6%. A positive read is wrong most of the time. A quarter of these tumours reading LR-5 is the failure mode that puts a cHCC-CCA onto an HCC transplant pathway undetected.

opts.name: Accept an atypical pattern as the finding and move to tissue
opts.when: In 30 pathology-proven cHCC-CCA from 891 consecutive liver resections, 70% showed imaging atypical for HCC — which is to say the pre-operative read did not identify HCC in most of them, and did in the remaining 30%.
opts.pref: Most patients. The useful output of imaging in this disease is 'this does not behave like HCC', which is a decision to biopsy and to involve pathology, not a diagnosis.
opts.avoid: Do not keep repeating imaging in the hope of a pattern that will not come. And do not over-read the 70%: it was derived retrospectively with the pathology already known, which inflates how readily atypia is spotted prospectively.

alt.order: Ordered by how much published data exist on each, not by a demonstrated difference in accuracy — no study compares these modalities head to head in this tumour. Every one of these series had pathological proof in every lesion, which means the lesions managed on imaging alone, the ones the criteria are aimed at, are absent from all three denominators. None of them is diagnostic, and the correct endpoint of all three is the same: a decision about tissue.
alt.flagnote: Ratification item: does the programme want a standing rule that an LR-M observation, or any observation with a mixed enhancement pattern, is reviewed by the transplant surgeon before any needle is passed? NCCN's HCC algorithm already carries the footnote 'if patient is a potential transplant candidate, consider referral to transplant center before biopsy'. Registry: imaging category assigned, biopsy route, and the final histology.

avoid.t: Do not accept "imaging characteristics consistent with intrahepatic mixed hepato-cholangiocarcinoma on CT or MRI" as a diagnostic criterion. There is no such imaging phenotype.
avoid.pref: Replace it with a histological criterion. The local Mixed Hepatocholangiocarcinoma CPG of 11 April 2022 states that criterion verbatim and then asks only for 'biopsy or cytology results demonstrating malignancy' — which is a criterion for cancer, not for this cancer. The OPTN review-board pathway that now governs the allocation request requires biopsy-proven mixed HCC-iCCA.
avoid.avoid: The practical consequence of the current wording is that a patient can satisfy the local protocol without any evidence of cholangiocytic differentiation at all, and then be submitted for an exception that requires it.
avoid.note: The 2019 WHO change made this worse rather than better: because subtypes with stem-cell features were redistributed to HCC and iCCA, the tumours now called cHCC-CCA are a narrower set than the ones most of the imaging literature describes.

avoid.t: Do not call two separate tumours — one HCC, one iCCA — in the same liver a cHCC-CCA.
avoid.pref: Report it as what it is: synchronous primary liver cancers. The WHO definition is one tumour containing both differentiations, and the fifth edition explicitly excludes the double-cancer and collision types from the category. In the 19-patient multicentre transplant series, the 8 patients with genuinely mixed tumours had a mean survival of 61.6 months against 15.5 months in the 11 with separate HCC and cholangiocarcinoma lesions (p=0.025) — on 8 and 11 patients, which is as readily a chance finding as a biological one.
avoid.avoid: The international very-early-iCCA study made mixed hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma in the same nodule an explicit exclusion criterion, and analysed 48 of the 81 explant cholangiocarcinomas it found among 25,016 transplants. Mixing true mixed tumours with separate synchronous primaries is the commonest way the published outcome figures in this disease become uninterpretable — and, as Gate 5 says, that same paper is the one whose 3 cm threshold now governs cHCC-CCA listing.

avoid.t: Do not let a radiomic or deep-learning classifier stand in for histology, however good its published performance.
avoid.pref: Treat these as research tools that may eventually tell you which component drives behaviour. A deep-learning model trained on HCC and iCCA whole-slide images reclassified 405 cHCC-CCA tumours as HCC-like or iCCA-like, and in the liver transplant subset the iCCA-like tumours had 5-year overall survival of 45.4% against 76.4% for the HCC-like ones, HR 2.69 (95% CI 1.15–6.31).
avoid.avoid: No such model is validated for a listing decision, an operative decision or a regimen choice, and none has been tested prospectively. There is also no ground truth: the model was trained on pathologist-assigned labels in a paper that simultaneously showed pathologists agree on the cHCC-CCA diagnosis at kappa 0.19 to 0.37, and the reclassification is done on resection or explant slides, which do not exist at listing. Nothing on this page should be done on a model output.
avoid.note: What the result does mean is uncomfortable and belongs at the board: if the entity splits into two groups 31 percentage points apart in 5-year post-transplant survival, then every pooled cHCC-CCA survival figure on this page is a weighted average of two diseases in unknown proportions.

gates.name: 1 · Tissue — one component does not exclude the other
crit: The destination is named before the needle: resection, the transplant pathway, or systemic therapy
Core needle biopsy rather than fine-needle aspiration wherever tissue is needed
Pathology told in advance that cHCC-CCA is the question, so both components are looked for and reported
Enough tissue preserved for multigene panel testing in advanced or recurrent disease
The report states which component predominates, and the margin, vascular and nodal findings
gates.ask: Do I need tissue for where this patient is going, and does a result showing one component mean anything about the other?

standard.t: A biopsy showing only HCC, or only cholangiocarcinoma, does not exclude the other component — the sampling problem is the central diagnostic fact of this disease.
standard.pref: Say this out loud at the board whenever a biopsy result is being used to route a patient. In 21 resected cHCC-CCA with pre-operative imaging and biopsy, a mixed imaging pattern was 48% sensitive and 81% specific, biopsy alone was 48% sensitive and 100% specific, and either test positive gave 60% sensitivity and 82% specificity. The mechanism is in the same paper: CK19 was positive in 33% of the biopsies but 84% of the corresponding surgical specimens, so the needle systematically under-detects the cholangiocytic component.
standard.avoid: Do not treat a single-component biopsy as a settled histology in a patient who is about to be listed, resected or started on a regimen chosen for that histology. NCCN says it directly: needle biopsies will not necessarily show both elements of the malignancy. In the 19-patient multicentre transplant series only 4 patients were biopsied before transplantation and all 4 were read as HCC — a sensitivity of 0 in that series.
standard.note: A specificity of 100% with a sensitivity of 48% means the result you can act on is a positive one. A biopsy reporting cHCC-CCA is almost certainly right; a biopsy reporting pure HCC in a tumour that looks wrong on imaging has told you very little. Both figures come from 21 cases against 21 controls, so the confidence intervals are wide and the 1:1 construction means the predictive values do not transfer to a surveillance population in which this tumour is 1–5% of nodules.

standard.t: If the transplant pathway is in play, tissue is mandatory, not optional — the OPTN review-board criteria require biopsy-proven mixed HCC-iCCA, and the transperitoneal-route prohibition you apply in perihilar disease does not carry over here.
standard.pref: Discuss the route with the transplant team before the needle, as NCCN's HCC algorithm advises, but obtain the tissue. The 2024 ILTS-ILCA consensus recommends biopsy in HCC transplant candidates specifically to rule out cholangiocarcinoma or a mixed tumour because it changes eligibility, prognosis and treatment (weak evidence, moderate strength).
standard.avoid: Do not import the perihilar cholangiocarcinoma rule — there, avoidance of transperitoneal biopsy is a condition of OPTN Policy 9.5.A and the Mayo protocol, and this is the perihilar CCA pathway's constraint, not this one. The local CPG's position, that transperitoneal aspiration or biopsy 'should be minimized but are not excluded', is the defensible one and is now reinforced by the requirement for biopsy proof.
standard.note: Grade D because no study measures seeding risk after biopsy of a cHCC-CCA, and none compares routes. The requirement for tissue is a policy fact; the safety of the route is an extrapolation from HCC and iCCA biopsy practice. The ILTS-ILCA statement is cited here from its abstract and the guidance table reproduced in the 2026 transplant overview, not from a full-text read.

standard.t: Send multigene panel testing on the diagnostic specimen in any patient whose disease is advanced, recurrent or likely to need systemic therapy.
standard.pref: Every advanced case, and preferably on the diagnostic rather than the explant specimen. NCCN states that panel testing should be considered in all patients with advanced-stage mixed tumours to identify targetable alterations associated with cholangiocarcinoma. In the largest genomic series — 150 cHCC-CCA against 2,372 HCC profiled commercially — potentially actionable alterations were found in 52 of 150 (34.7%) against 462 of 2,372 HCC (19.5%), the 59 alterations comprising IDH1 or IDH2 in 16, FGFR2 in 11, BRCA1 or BRCA2 in 7, ERBB2 in 5, BRAF in 4 and MET in 3. In a separate 72-case series FGFR2 alteration was found in 26.4% and strong HER2 protein expression in 8.3%, on 19 and 6 patients respectively.
standard.avoid: Do not expect microsatellite instability or mismatch-repair deficiency to be the answer, and do not make them the only test ordered: all 72 tumours in one series were mismatch-repair proficient, no deficiency was found in any of 24 cHCC-CCA in another (2 of 97 primary liver carcinomas overall, both iCCA), and only 4 of 150 (2.7%) were tumour-mutational-burden high at a median burden of 2.5 mutations per megabase. Note what 0 of 24 actually licenses: an upper 95% bound of about 14%, so this is uncommon rather than absent.
standard.note: The genomic argument that cHCC-CCA is 'really HCC' has to be stated more carefully after the large series. TERT promoter and TP53 alterations do predominate — TP53 60.0% in cHCC-CCA against 36.9% in HCC, TERT promoter 50.0% against 59.3% — and in 20 microdissected tumours TERT promoter mutation was present in both components, establishing clonal common origin. But CTNNB1, the classic HCC driver, was under 7% against over 34% in HCC, and the iCCA-typical drivers are present at low frequency: IDH1 8.0% against 0.3%, IDH2 2.7% against 0.04% and FGFR2 7.3% against 0.3%. That directly contradicts the 20-tumour series that found no IDH1, IDH2, FGFR2 or BAP1 at all, which with 20 cases could not exclude frequencies below about 15%. Cite both. The practical point is that a biliary target is uncommon but real, and you will not find it without the panel.

opts.name: Core needle biopsy of the index lesion
opts.when: NCCN lists raised CA 19-9 or CEA with suspicion of iCCA or cHCC-CCA as an indication for core needle biopsy even in a lesion that meets imaging criteria for HCC, and lists biopsy for any lesion highly suspicious for malignancy that does not meet HCC imaging features.
opts.pref: The patient whose destination depends on histology: a transplant pathway candidate, a patient in whom a systemic regimen must be chosen, a non-cirrhotic patient with an LR-5 pattern.
opts.avoid: Obtain it before ablation if ablation is contemplated, because the opportunity closes. A negative result for the second component changes nothing.

opts.name: Proceed to resection without tissue
opts.when: NCCN's Principles of Surgery for intrahepatic biliary disease state that a pre-operative biopsy is not always necessary before a definitive potentially curative resection, and that a suspicious mass in the proper clinical setting should be treated as malignant. Surgical resection without core needle biopsy should be considered with multidisciplinary review.
opts.pref: The fit patient with a resectable mass in whom the operation would not change whichever histology came back — because the operation this page recommends, anatomical resection with regional lymphadenectomy, covers both components.
opts.avoid: Do not use it to skip the transplant question in a cirrhotic patient with a small tumour, and do not use it when the plan includes an extent of lymphadenectomy that depends on the answer. A resection done without tissue makes the diagnosis but forfeits the option of starting on the OPTN pathway, which needs biopsy proof and six months of stability.

opts.name: Repeat biopsy at recurrence or progression
opts.when: NCCN recommends considering repeat biopsy in metastatic or locally advanced recurrence after prior resection or local therapy, to establish the dominant histology at recurrence, and again at progression where areas of response and progression are discordant.
opts.pref: Any recurrence in which an isolated HCC or cholangiocarcinoma component would change the regimen, in a patient still fit for further systemic therapy.
opts.avoid: Do not re-biopsy when the result would not change the plan, and do not assume the recurrence carries the same component mix as the primary. The sampling problem of this gate applies unchanged to the recurrence, and no study has measured how often a recurrence biopsy in this disease reproduces the primary's histology.

alt.order: Ordered by how often each is the right first move, not by evidence of superiority — there is no comparative study of biopsy strategy in this disease. What drives the order is the destination: a transplant pathway needs tissue, a resection usually does not, and a recurrence often needs it again.
alt.flagnote: Ratification item: does a biopsy reporting pure HCC in a tumour with discordant markers or imaging close the cHCC-CCA question for this programme, or does the board record it as unresolved and plan on that basis? With 48% sensitivity, 100% specificity and CK19 positive in 33% of biopsies against 84% of the matching specimens, those are materially different operating rules and the group has to pick one. A second question follows: who re-reads the slide? In the large genomic series, 117 cases called HCC that carried iCCA-typical alterations were sent for histopathological re-review and the HCC diagnosis was confirmed in only 48 (41%), being changed to iCCA in 23, to cHCC-CCA in 13 and to gallbladder carcinoma in 1, with 32 left indeterminate. Audit: pre-operative histology against explant or resection histology, every case.

avoid.t: Do not accept a fine-needle aspirate reporting malignancy as the histological basis for a cHCC-CCA diagnosis.
avoid.pref: Core needle biopsy, with architecture, and with the pathologist told what the question is. The diagnosis is morphological and depends on seeing two differentiations in one tumour, which a cytological preparation is poorly placed to show, and the consensus that created the definition is a pathology document that says so.
avoid.avoid: The local CPG's diagnostic criterion accepts cytology showing malignancy. That satisfies neither the WHO definition nor the OPTN requirement for biopsy-proven mixed histology, and it is the single wording on the local document most likely to produce a declined exception request.

gates.name: 2 · Stage it as a biliary cancer, not as HCC
crit: Multiphase CT or MRI of the liver and abdomen, plus CT of the chest
Regional nodal status recorded explicitly — porta hepatis, gastrohepatic, periduodenal and peripancreatic stations
AJCC 8th edition intrahepatic bile duct T, N and M categories assigned, not a BCLC stage alone
Which component predominates, stated as a proportion where the specimen allows it
Baseline AFP and CA 19-9, with the date and clinical state at which each was drawn
gates.ask: Which staging system am I actually in, and have I looked at the nodes?

standard.t: Stage with the AJCC 8th edition intrahepatic bile duct system: it explicitly covers combined hepatocellular cholangiocarcinoma, and it is the system that has a nodal category.
standard.pref: Every case, from the first board. The 8th edition states that all intrahepatic bile duct carcinomas, including combined hepatocellular cholangiocarcinomas, are covered by that staging system, and the NCCN Biliary Tract Cancers guideline reproduces the tables. T1a is a solitary tumour 5 cm or less without vascular invasion; T1b solitary above 5 cm; T2 solitary with intrahepatic vascular invasion or multiple tumours; T3 perforation of the visceral peritoneum; T4 direct invasion of local extrahepatic structures. Any N1 is stage IIIB.
standard.avoid: Do not stage this with BCLC and stop — BCLC has no nodal category at all, and nodal disease is one of the two findings that most changes what you can offer. But do not treat the AJCC stage as the prognosis either. In the 40-recipient Korean registry series neither pre-transplant Milan status, nor tumour number, nor maximum tumour size predicted overall or recurrence-free survival, while perineural invasion (HR 5.14, 95% CI 1.07–24.69), portal vein tumour thrombosis (HR 13.43, 95% CI 2.17–83.21) and microvascular invasion (HR 4.56, 95% CI 1.36–15.22) did — all of them explant findings. Record the stage and the pathological variables separately.
standard.note: Regional nodes for the intrahepatic bile duct system are those associated with the hilar hepatic artery, portal vein and cystic duct, and the inferior phrenic, gastrohepatic, periduodenal and peripancreatic regions. Downgraded from B to C on the full-text read: the sentence covering combined tumours was confirmed only from NCCN's reproduction of the AJCC tables and not from the manual, and no study has validated this staging system in this histology. The hazard ratios above rest on 4, 3 and 19 patients respectively and are directional only. See the quick reference.

standard.t: Image the chest, and look specifically for nodal disease — the lymph node is the second commonest site of first recurrence in this tumour, which is not true of HCC.
standard.pref: Every case. In a single-centre Japanese series of 19 resected cHCC-CCA, the tumour behaved like a biliary cancer in this respect: the liver was the commonest recurrence site but the lymph node was second, where in HCC it is not, and biliary invasion was present in 36.8% against 5.0% of the institution's HCC resections. The narrative surgical literature puts nodal metastasis in cHCC-CCA at 25–35%. Where nodal recurrence happens, it concentrates proximally: in a mapping study of 53 patients whose first recurrence after resection of a primary liver cancer was in regional nodes, the hepatic hilum was involved in 62.3% and the portal vein–vena cava region in 39.6%.
standard.avoid: Do not accept a staging package built for HCC. A liver-only protocol with no chest imaging and no deliberate nodal assessment will miss the two findings that most often change the plan. And read the mapping study for what it is: only 11 of its 53 patients had cHCC-CCA, the denominator is patients who recurred in nodes rather than patients at risk, so the percentages describe where disease goes and not how likely it is to go there, and the median node count at the original operation was 6.
standard.note: The local CPG asks for CT of the chest, contrasted liver-protocol MR of the abdomen and pelvis, and an MR bone survey, with FDG-PET added where CA 19-9 is raised and other imaging shows no metastasis. The chest and liver imaging are standard practice; the routine MR bone survey appears in no guideline and is not supported by comparative data — see the honest section.

standard.t: Record which component predominates, with a proportion where the specimen allows it, because the proportion tracks outcome.
standard.pref: Every resection and explant report. In a four-centre cohort of 306 resected tumours classified by three blinded pathologists on a standardised sampling protocol and split at 70%, median recurrence-free survival was 1.02 years in the 93 HCC-dominant patients, 0.36 years in the 101 balanced and 0.30 years in the 112 CCA-dominant, with median overall survival 3.16, 1.93 and 1.86 years and 5-year overall survival 46.1%, 26.1% and 28.3%. Component proportion stayed independent for recurrence-free survival (balanced HR 1.495, CCA-dominant HR 1.487) and overall survival (HR 1.428 and 1.447), C-index 0.712 and 0.650.
standard.avoid: Do not treat the proportion as a validated classifier, and do not present it as three groups. The only significant contrasts were HCC-dominant against the other two; balanced and CCA-dominant were indistinguishable (recurrence-free survival p=0.592, overall survival p=0.822), so the finding is really binary. WHO 2019 sets no proportion threshold, the 2018 consensus deliberately set none, the 70% cut-off was borrowed from conventions in mixed neuroendocrine, breast and myeloproliferative neoplasms rather than derived here, and the 30% cholangiocytic cut-off from a 72-case series was derived by ROC on the same cohort it was then tested in, at AUC 0.717. They are different numbers from different datasets and they will not agree on the same tumour.
standard.note: The proportion is the most promising available handle on which backbone to borrow in systemic therapy, and it is the reason to ask for it on every report even while it is not yet a decision rule. Two limits are worth saying out loud: it can only be measured on a resected specimen, so it cannot inform the pre-operative decision; and in the one advanced-disease cohort that tested it, HCC-dominant and iCCA-dominant tumours treated identically did not differ in survival at any threshold from 20% to 80%. Prognostic is not predictive.

alt.t: Add FDG-PET where CA 19-9 is raised and cross-sectional imaging shows no metastatic disease, and biopsy a suspicious extrahepatic lesion rather than assuming it.
alt.pref: The patient about to enter a six-month transplant pathway or a major hepatectomy, in whom an occult extrahepatic deposit would change everything. This is the local CPG's own position and it is a reasonable use of a test with poor performance in HCC and better performance in biliary disease.
alt.avoid: Do not use PET to make the primary diagnosis, and do not treat a negative PET as exclusion of nodal disease. NCCN does not recommend FDG-PET for routine staging in HCC, and no study has measured its performance in cHCC-CCA specifically.
alt.note: Grade D, and on the full-text read this item now carries no primary citation at all, because the paper previously attached to it is a contrast-enhanced ultrasound study with no PET content. The recommendation is the local document's requirement plus mechanistic reasoning from biliary disease, with no comparative outcome data in this histology and none in any histology reported here.

alt.t: Sample a radiologically suspicious regional node by endoscopic ultrasound before committing to a six-month transplant pathway.
alt.pref: A potential transplant pathway candidate with suspicious porta hepatis nodes. Nodal disease is an exclusion in the local protocol and in every published series, so a positive nodal result does not cost candidacy that existed — it identifies a patient who was never a candidate, before six months of therapy and a workup are spent.
alt.avoid: Do not let a nodal pass become a pass at the primary if you have reason to keep the primary untouched; they are different sampling targets with different consequences. And note there are no morphological criteria that reliably identify a malignant node, so a 'suspicious node' trigger is a soft one.
alt.note: This is the local CPG's requirement, written as 'if possible'. It is sound logic with no comparative data behind it, and the ILTS-ILCA consensus attached to it is cited from its abstract rather than from a full-text read.

avoid.t: Do not use the Milan criteria as a stage.
avoid.pref: Record the AJCC stage, and record separately whether the radiological tumour burden falls within Milan, because the published transplant series use Milan as an enrolment limit and the allocation pathway uses a 3 cm solitary limit. They are three different measurements of the same patient and the page keeps them apart deliberately.
avoid.avoid: And know that the radiological measurement is wrong in this tumour in one direction. In 19 transplant recipients whose explants showed cHCC-CCA, 84.2% were within Milan on pre-transplant imaging but only 36.8% remained within Milan on explant pathology (p=0.01 against the matched controls). Imaging-based Milan systematically understages this disease — and imaging-based Milan is exactly the classification the 12-centre transplant analysis used, applied retrospectively at diagnosis for uniformity of analysis rather than as a prospective selection rule, and never validated as a stage in this histology.

avoid.t: Do not carry an HCC surveillance-and-staging pathway into this disease once the histology is known.
avoid.pref: Switch to the biliary framework: nodal assessment, chest imaging, CA 19-9, and the expectation of early and nodal recurrence. Outcomes sit between HCC and cholangiocarcinoma — in the Taiwan Cancer Registry, among 95,149 primary liver cancers, 5-year overall survival for the combined tumour was 25.7%, intermediate between HCC and intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, with 55.5% of the combined group resected and tumour grade unrecorded in 68.7% of the registry entries.
avoid.avoid: Nor should the staging shift become an excuse for pessimism: in 529 SEER patients the median overall survival was 8 months, but that is a whole-registry figure dominated by unresected disease and is not the figure for a resected patient. Neither registry paper should be quoted beyond its descriptive survival. The SEER analysis contains two unreconciled internal contradictions — its abstract states the higher incidence is in women while its text and table report 0.08 per 100,000 in men against 0.03 in women, and the hazard ratio for surgery is 4.94 in the abstract and 4.18 in the table — and in the Taiwan registry the hazard ratio for TACE was 0.56 in the non-surgical stratum and 1.64 in the surgical one, which is the signature of confounding by indication rather than a treatment effect.

gates.name: 3 · Resectable disease
crit: A single tumour, or limited multifocal disease in a highly selected patient, with a technically achievable negative margin
No nodal disease beyond the porta hepatis, no peritoneal disease, no distant metastasis
Future liver remnant and hepatic reserve adequate for the resection the margin requires
Patient fit for an anatomical hepatectomy with regional lymphadenectomy, at a centre that performs them
The patient has been told what the recurrence figures in this histology actually are
gates.ask: Can I get a negative margin with a regional lymphadenectomy, and has the patient been told what recurrence looks like in this disease?

standard.t: Anatomical liver resection to a negative margin, with regional lymphadenectomy, is the only established curative treatment — resection is the standard of care for resectable disease in both NCCN guidelines that address it.
standard.pref: Any patient who meets the criteria above. Both the NCCN Hepatocellular Carcinoma and Biliary Tract Cancers guidelines state that liver resection is considered the standard treatment for resectable mixed HCC-CCA, and the contemporary surgical review puts 5-year overall survival after R0 resection at 25–40% with recurrence in more than 60%. On the margin the evidence is not uniform: in an 80-patient Korean hepatectomy series patients with a wide margin did significantly better than those with an R1 resection or a margin of 2 mm or less, while series using a 1 cm cut-off found margin width non-significant.
standard.avoid: Do not offer a non-anatomical wedge where an anatomical resection is achievable, and do not accept a planned close margin. Grade C and not higher because every supporting series is retrospective, single- or few-centre, and none randomises anything — no prospective trial of resection has ever been conducted in this disease. The surgical review that frames the operation is explicit that it manages cHCC-CCA according to oncologic principles developed for intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, and it does not discuss transplantation at all.
standard.note: In the first large Western series, 27 patients had a 5-year overall survival of 24% after resection — in a cohort with a 0% rate of cirrhosis, which is why it cannot be set beside the Asian and European transplant series where 60–90% are cirrhotic and hepatitis-B-related. Patients never operated on do not appear in its denominator, and it predates the 2018 consensus and the 2019 WHO classification entirely, so an unknown fraction of those 27 would now be reclassified as small-duct iCCA or excluded as collision tumours. It is still quoted as the baseline poor-prognosis figure in 2026 papers. [EXPERTISE]

standard.t: Expect early recurrence, and say the numbers before the operation rather than after it.
standard.pref: Every consent conversation. In a 95-patient multicentre radical-resection cohort median overall survival was 26.8 months, median recurrence-free survival 7.27 months and 5-year overall survival 23.6%. In 19 tumours resected at a single Japanese centre, 5-year overall survival was 44.7% against 56.6% for HCC and 38.5% for iCCA — differences that did not reach significance, which with 19 patients is uninformative rather than reassuring — while 5-year recurrence-free survival was only 12.2%. In 30 resected tumours from 891 consecutive resections, cHCC-CCA independently predicted worse disease-free survival (HR 3.146, 95% CI 1.854–5.339) and worse overall survival (HR 2.320, 95% CI 1.134–4.747) against HCC, with 5-year disease-free survival 37.3% against 58.3% for HCC and 32.0% for iCCA.
standard.avoid: Do not quote HCC recurrence figures. The one variable that separates a good outcome from a poor one in the largest single-institution series is lymphovascular invasion: 5-year overall survival was 93.3% without it and 35.8% with it in 80 patients, HR 11.35 — with a 95% confidence interval from 3.20 to 40.3, so the direction is secure and the magnitude is not. That same series reported a median overall survival of 85.1 months and 5-year survival of 56.4%, roughly double every other resection cohort here, which points to an unusually early and well-compensated surgical population rather than to better surgery. Do not use it as the resection benchmark in a transplant comparison.
standard.note: Independent predictors of overall survival in the 95-patient cohort were CA 19-9 of 37 U/mL or more (HR 8.68, p=0.002), Child-Pugh above 5 (HR 5.52, p=0.027), more than one tumour (HR 30.85, p=0.002), tumour size, and post-operative TACE (HR 0.2, p=0.005). Read those as direction at most, and preferably not at all: no confidence intervals are reported, a hazard ratio of 30.85 in a 95-patient Cox model is a sparse-data artefact, and the same model returns an AFP of 200 or more as protective for recurrence-free survival (HR 0.45), which is not biologically credible and most likely marks HCC-dominant tumours that received HCC-directed adjuvant treatment.

alt.t: A minimally invasive approach is reasonable in a well-selected patient, provided it does not compromise the margin or the nodal dissection.
alt.pref: Peripheral tumours in a fit patient at a centre with the laparoscopic or robotic volume. NCCN's Principles of Surgery for intrahepatic disease state that minimally invasive approaches by experienced surgeons have been shown to be safe and effective in well-selected cases.
alt.avoid: Do not let the approach dictate the lymphadenectomy. The published comparisons of minimally invasive and open resection in intrahepatic biliary malignancy specifically exclude or do not separately report cHCC-CCA, so the oncological comparability claim is borrowed.

alt.t: In a cirrhotic patient with a small tumour, decide resection against transplantation as one question rather than two — this is Gate 5, and taking the knife to the liver first may close it.
alt.pref: Any cirrhotic patient with a tumour of 3 cm or less in whom both operations are technically possible. In a three-centre French study of cirrhotic patients with iCCA or cHCC-CCA of 5 cm or less, 49 transplanted patients had lower recurrence than 26 resected patients (18% versus 46%, p=0.01) and higher 5-year recurrence-free survival (75% versus 36%, p=0.004). Note which endpoint moved: 5-year overall survival was 67% against 40% and did not reach significance (p=0.17). The protective hazard ratio for transplantation, 0.23 (95% CI 0.07–0.82, p=0.02), comes from a multivariable model in the 2–5 cm subgroup of 24 transplant against 21 resection patients.
alt.avoid: Do not read that as a treatment effect, and this time the authors say so themselves. A known cholangiocarcinoma diagnosis was an absolute contraindication to transplantation throughout the study period, so all 49 transplant diagnoses were made on the explant — 44 had been listed for HCC and 5 for decompensated cirrhosis. The transplant arm waited a median of 394 days from diagnosis to surgery against 131 days in the resection arm, which the authors state inevitably selected tumours that had not progressed, and 63% of them had pre-operative TACE against 15% of the resected patients. There was no intention-to-treat analysis and no dropout denominator. Read Gate 5 before the decision is made.
alt.note: The local CPG does allow a prior attempted resection onto the transplant pathway, provided there has been a sustained response to neoadjuvant therapy for at least six months after the most recent intervention.

avoid.t: Do not offer resection for nodal disease beyond the porta hepatis, or for multifocal disease outside a highly selected case.
avoid.pref: Route these patients to Gate 7. NCCN's Principles of Surgery for intrahepatic disease are explicit: lymph node metastases beyond the porta hepatis and distant metastatic disease contraindicate resection, gross nodal metastases to the porta hepatis portend a poor prognosis and resection should only be considered in highly selected cases, and multifocal liver disease is generally representative of metastatic disease.
avoid.avoid: Those statements were written for intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma. Applying them to cHCC-CCA is an extrapolation — but it is the extrapolation that matches this tumour's nodal recurrence pattern, which is biliary rather than hepatocellular.

avoid.t: Do not promise an HCC outcome to a resected patient because the tumour is HCC-predominant.
avoid.pref: Give the figures for this histology and for the component proportion if it is known. Even the HCC-dominant group in the 306-patient proportion study had a median recurrence-free survival of 1.02 years and a 5-year overall survival of 46.1%.
avoid.avoid: Population-level figures are worse again and should not be quoted to a resection candidate either: 529 SEER patients had a median survival of 8 months and the Taiwan registry gave 5-year overall survival of 25.7%, but both are dominated by patients who were never resected.

gates.name: 4 · The node question in theatre
crit: cHCC-CCA known or suspected before the operation, on histology, markers or imaging
A pre-operative diagnosis of HCC in a patient whose CA 19-9, CEA or enhancement pattern raises cholangiocytic differentiation
Radiologically suspicious porta hepatis nodes
An intra-operative finding — a firm, pale or desmoplastic tumour — that does not look like HCC
gates.ask: Am I taking the porta hepatis nodes, and if I am not, can I write down why?

standard.t: Perform a regional lymphadenectomy of the porta hepatis when cHCC-CCA is known or suspected, and record the number of nodes retrieved and the number involved.
standard.pref: Every resection in which the histology is known or suspected pre-operatively. NCCN's Principles of Surgery for intrahepatic biliary disease state that a regional lymphadenectomy of the porta hepatis is carried out; the contemporary surgical review makes nodal dissection part of the definition of a potentially curative operation and puts nodal metastasis in cHCC-CCA at 25–35%; and where nodal recurrence occurs it concentrates at the hepatic hilum, involved in 62.3% of the 53 patients in the mapping study whose first recurrence was nodal.
standard.avoid: Do not make the dissection contingent on how the tumour looks: the whole problem of this gate is that the histology is usually not known until afterwards. Nodal status is also an AJCC category — N1 is stage IIIB regardless of T — so an unsampled node leaves the patient unstaged rather than node-negative.
standard.note: Grade C, and the honest position is that no study has shown that lymphadenectomy improves survival in cHCC-CCA. The case for it is staging information, the nodal recurrence pattern, and concordance with the iCCA guideline that governs the staging system. The mapping study it leans on had only 11 cHCC-CCA patients among 53, counts recurrences rather than patients at risk, and was designed to define radiotherapy volumes. It is not a demonstrated survival benefit.

standard.t: Where cHCC-CCA was not suspected and no nodes were taken, write that in the operative note as a decision with a reason, not as an omission.
standard.pref: Every hepatectomy for presumed HCC. This matters because the next surgeon, the pathologist and the board all need to know whether pNx means 'judged unnecessary' or 'not considered'. In a 179-patient single-centre cohort of curative resections for intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma including 77 cHCC-CCA, node dissection was performed in only 54 (30%) and reached the 6-node adequacy standard in only 14 of those 54 (26%); the only independent driver of the decision to dissect was a pre-operative diagnosis of cholangiocarcinoma (OR 3.33, 95% CI 1.54–7.34, p=0.002), present in 70% of the dissected group against 29% of the undissected. The dissection followed the label, not the tumour.
standard.avoid: Do not leave the nodal status silent. A pNx specimen in a tumour that turns out to be cHCC-CCA is the commonest avoidable information loss in this disease.

opts.name: Routine regional lymphadenectomy
opts.when: What the guideline wording supports: NCCN carries out a regional lymphadenectomy of the porta hepatis for intrahepatic biliary malignancy, and the narrative reviews of surgical management of cHCC-CCA make R0 resection with regional node dissection the standard.
opts.pref: Any patient in whom cHCC-CCA is known or suspected pre-operatively, and any patient in whom staging information will change adjuvant or surveillance decisions.
opts.avoid: Do not extend it beyond the porta hepatis as a routine. The nodal mapping study put the para-aortic 16a1, 16a2 and 16b1 regions and the splenic artery and hilum below 10% recurrence, and found no recurrence at all in the para-oesophageal or 16b2 regions.

opts.name: Selective lymphadenectomy on intra-operative judgement
opts.when: A single-centre cohort of 179 curative hepatectomies — 102 pure cholangiocarcinoma and 77 cHCC-CCA — reported that selective dissection on clinical judgement did not compromise overall survival: median overall survival was 59.1 months in the undissected group against 30.5 months pN0 and 17.4 months pN1 (p=0.007), with no adjusted difference between pNx and pN0 (HR 0.78, 95% CI 0.46–1.30, p=0.34).
opts.pref: The HCC-predominant tumour in a cirrhotic patient where hilar dissection carries real morbidity, and the patient in whom the nodal result would not change management.
opts.avoid: Read the whole paper, because its other endpoint runs the other way: after adjustment, pNx was an independent adverse factor for progression-free survival (HR 2.12, 95% CI 1.20–3.77, p=0.012). The 59.1-month median in the undissected group is the selection the study is examining — 54% of pNx patients were cHCC-CCA against 19% of the dissected, their tumours were smaller (3.0 against 4.0 cm), earlier staged and less often perineurally invaded, and CA 19-9 was missing in 70% of them. Only 26% of the dissections met the 6-node standard, so the pN0 group is contaminated by understaged patients, which biases the comparison toward no difference. And the cHCC-CCA subgroup analyses, on 77 patients, were all non-significant. Downgraded to D: this is not evidence of equivalence in this histology.

opts.name: No nodal dissection
opts.when: Defensible only where the pre-operative diagnosis was HCC, the tumour behaved like HCC, and cHCC-CCA was not on the differential.
opts.pref: Nothing, once the diagnosis is suspected. This option exists on the page because it is what happens to most of these patients in practice, not because it is recommended.
opts.avoid: It leaves the patient unstaged in the system that AJCC says applies to them, it removes the nodal variable from every subsequent adjuvant and surveillance decision, and in the one cohort that examined it, omitting the dissection was independently associated with worse adjusted progression-free survival (HR 2.12, 95% CI 1.20–3.77).

alt.order: The order reflects guideline wording, not a survival advantage: no study in cHCC-CCA compares nodal strategies with an outcome endpoint, and the one cohort that addresses selective dissection is retrospective, has the indication confounded by the pre-operative label, reaches opposite conclusions on its two endpoints, and is non-significant in its own cHCC-CCA subgroup. What the order does reflect is that the staging information is lost irreversibly if the nodes are not taken.
alt.flagnote: Ratification item: does this programme adopt routine porta hepatis lymphadenectomy for every resection in which cHCC-CCA is known or suspected, as the iCCA guideline would, or a selective policy with a documented reason in each case? This is a live choice and the evidence does not settle it — the single cohort usually cited for selective dissection shows no adjusted difference in overall survival and a significantly worse adjusted progression-free survival without dissection. A second decision follows from it: whether a pre-operative diagnosis of HCC with a raised CA 19-9 is enough to trigger the dissection. A third: what counts as an adequate harvest, given that only 26% of dissections in that cohort reached 6 nodes. Audit: nodes retrieved and nodes involved, by pre-operative diagnosis, with nodal recurrence at two years.

avoid.t: Do not extend the dissection to the para-aortic or splenic regions as a routine.
avoid.pref: Confine the dissection to the porta hepatis and the portal vein–vena cava region, which carried 62.3% and 39.6% of first nodal recurrences in the mapping study.
avoid.avoid: Recurrence in the para-aortic 16a1, 16a2 and 16b1 regions and in the splenic artery and hilum was under 10%, and there was none in the para-oesophageal or 16b2 regions. Downgraded to D: that study maps where recurrence appeared in 53 patients of whom only 11 had cHCC-CCA, its denominator is patients who recurred in nodes rather than patients at risk, the median node count at the original operation was 6 so some apparent recurrences are residual disease in stations nobody dissected, and it was designed to define radiotherapy target volumes rather than the extent of an operation. It is directional evidence about where disease goes, not a trial of dissection extent.

gates.name: 5 · Transplant — ask which document governs the listing
crit: Cirrhosis, with disease unresectable on technical grounds or because of the underlying liver
Biopsy-proven cHCC-CCA or mixed HCC-iCCA, solitary and 3 cm or less, to meet the OPTN review-board criteria
Six months of documented stability on locoregional or systemic therapy, no new lesions, no extrahepatic disease
Well or moderately differentiated, with no macrovascular invasion and no nodal disease
A programme that has written down which criteria it is using, and a registry that records every case
gates.ask: Does this patient meet the criteria of the document that will actually govern the listing — not the criteria of the paper I read?

standard.t: Ask the transplant question at the first board, before a resection attempt or a long course of palliative systemic therapy forecloses it.
standard.pref: Every cirrhotic patient with a small tumour, and every patient in whom the histology is known or suspected and the liver will not tolerate the resection a negative margin requires. The published advantage of transplantation over resection in this disease is confined to small-tumour, cirrhotic populations, which is precisely the group a resection attempt removes from the pathway.
standard.avoid: The sequencing recommendation rests on eligibility criteria and on the direction of retrospective comparisons, not on any trial of referral timing — that study does not exist and will not. It also rests on cohorts that cannot speak to a deliberate decision: in the 12-centre analysis only 2 of 99 transplant recipients were knowingly transplanted with the diagnosis, and in the French cirrhosis study a known cholangiocarcinoma diagnosis was an absolute contraindication, so all 49 transplants were explant diagnoses.
standard.note: The local CPG does permit a prior attempted resection, provided there has been a sustained response to neoadjuvant therapy for at least six months after the most recent intervention. That is more permissive than the perihilar protocol, where surgical violation of the tumour plane is an exclusion.

standard.t: Use the OPTN National Liver Review Board transplant-oncology criteria as the operative threshold, because those are the criteria the exception request will be judged against — biopsy-proven mixed HCC-iCCA, solitary and 3 cm or less, cirrhosis, unresectable, six months of stability after locoregional or systemic therapy, no extrahepatic disease, score MMaT-3.
standard.pref: Every listing decision. The guidance also sets the extension rule: imaging every three months confirming the tumour remains 3 cm or less with no extrahepatic disease. Confirm the current OPTN text before any listing decision — this page reflects the guidance as retrieved on 6 October 2026 and the document carries no printed version line.
standard.avoid: Do not plan a pathway against the local CPG's criteria and then discover at submission that they do not match. The local document, approved 11 April 2022, states that candidates are eligible 'regardless of size', does not require cirrhosis, and asks only for biopsy or cytology showing malignancy rather than mixed histology. It also states that the MELD exception application will be made 'once the exception is available from UNOS' — it is now available, and it is narrower than the protocol.
standard.note: Mind the distinction between referral and allocation. NCCN sets no size limit and says patients whose tumour is limited in size by centre-specific criteria should be evaluated at a transplant centre; the OPTN pathway sets 3 cm; the published series used Milan. A patient can be reasonably referred, reasonably transplanted under a local protocol, and still fail the exception criteria. Know where the 3 cm came from: it is an extrapolation from the 17-centre 'very early' intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma study, which excluded mixed hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma in the same nodule by design, defined its favourable group on explant pathology in 15 patients of whom 46.7% were incidental findings, and supports the 3 cm extension on an intermediate subgroup of 6 patients with 61% 5-year survival. Grade D is generous. [TX-TIMING] [PAYER]

alt.t: Transplantation for cHCC-CCA within Milan criteria, under a written protocol with prospective registry entry.
alt.pref: A cirrhotic patient with small-volume, node-negative, well or moderately differentiated disease at a programme that has written its criteria down. In the 12-centre retrospective analysis, 67 patients transplanted for cHCC-CCA within Milan had 5-year overall survival of 70.1% against 73.4% for 1,814 HCC recipients (p=0.806) and disease-free survival of 70.1% against 70.3% (p=0.740), while 5-year recurrence was double: 23.1% against 11.5%, p<0.001. Within Milan, transplantation gave better 5-year disease-free survival than resection (70.3% against 33.6%, p<0.001) but not better overall survival (70.1% against 49.7%, p=0.078). Beyond UCSF criteria 5-year overall survival was 15.8% against 67.3% for HCC. In 32 Korean recipients whose tumours were all found incidentally on the explant, 5-year recurrence was 32.2% and survival 65.8% overall, and 13.3% and 93.3% in the 15 with one or two tumours of 2 cm or less.
alt.avoid: Do not read any of this as a licence to list a diagnosed cHCC-CCA, because almost nobody in it was. Only 11 of 208 patients in the 12-centre analysis had a pre-operative diagnosis of cHCC-CCA and only 2 of those 11 were transplanted; 84 of the 99 transplant recipients had been pre-diagnosed as HCC. The survival 'equivalence' is a non-significant p value in a subgroup of 67, and the significant finding in that same subgroup is that recurrence was double. Milan status was assigned on initial imaging, which in this tumour understages: 84.2% within Milan on imaging fell to 36.8% on explant in a separate matched series. At the Korean centre, patients with a pre-operative diagnosis were principally excluded from transplantation, so that cohort is incidental by construction; its resection comparator was restricted to single 1–4 cm R0 node-negative tumours and still showed no transplant advantage (survival p=0.91, recurrence p=0.22), and post-recurrence survival was significantly worse after transplantation (median 9 against 21 months, p=0.016). The SEER comparison favouring transplantation within Milan rests on 15 matched pairs (p=0.015), 32 pairs overall (p=0.022), and 9 pairs beyond Milan where there was no difference (p=0.340), with Metavir fibrosis stage known in only 120 of 736 patients. Downgraded from C to D for that reason: there is no cohort of any size describing patients deliberately listed with this diagnosis.
alt.note: The updated meta-analysis of six retrospective comparative studies, now read in full, gives a pooled odds ratio of 0.55 (95% CI 0.38–0.81, p=0.002, I²=0%) for 5-year overall survival favouring transplantation, with the 1-year (0.67, 0.39–1.15) and 3-year (0.70, 0.42–1.17) estimates not significant, and recurrence-free odds ratios of 0.48 at one year and 0.40 at five. Four things qualify it: mean tumour size was 2.19–2.57 cm in the transplant arms against 2.7–6.26 cm in the resection arms, only one of the six studies used propensity matching, leave-one-out analysis flipped the significance of both the 3- and the 5-year overall survival estimates, and the 12-centre analysis contributes 99 of the 215 pooled transplant patients. Nearly all patients in both arms were pathological stage I or II (94.8% against 91.4%), so none of it speaks to beyond-criteria disease. The authors' own conclusion is that transplantation 'could be considered in carefully selected patients' and that the apparent advantage may be selection rather than treatment.

alt.t: Differentiation grade and the explant pathological variables carry the most reproducible signal in the transplant literature — but every one of them is measured after the organ is out.
alt.pref: Every candidacy discussion. In the three-centre French cirrhosis cohort, poor differentiation was independently predictive of recurrence in the 2–5 cm subgroup (HR 4.16, 95% CI 1.37–12.66, p=0.01) alongside nodule diameter (HR 1.10, 95% CI 1.02–1.73). In 40 Korean registry recipients, microvascular invasion was the only independent predictor of recurrence-free survival (HR 4.56, 95% CI 1.36–15.22) while perineural invasion (HR 5.14, 95% CI 1.07–24.69) and portal vein tumour thrombosis (HR 13.43, 95% CI 2.17–83.21) predicted worse overall survival — and in that cohort no pre-operative variable predicted anything.
alt.avoid: The problem is that all of these are explant variables. Pre-transplant biopsy grading of a tumour with two components is unreliable, the biopsy may sample only one component, and no study has tested whether biopsy grade predicts explant grade in this disease. So this is the right criterion measured at the wrong time, and the page should not pretend otherwise. The hazard ratios above also rest on 45, 19, 4 and 3 patients respectively, with confidence intervals to match.
alt.note: The 2018 propensity-matched series of 12 recipients, on which the local protocol rests, was not obtained for this revision and is not cited here as read. Its figures are taken from the 2026 transplant overview's secondary report of it: 5-year recurrence-free survival 42% against 44% when matched on explant pathology (p=0.45), but 28% against 61% when matched on pre-transplant characteristics (p=0.12). The direction of that asymmetry is the whole argument — matched on what you know before transplant, the cHCC-CCA patients did worse — and it points the same way as the 2026 double-matched cohort in the avoid column below. A separate 2026 comparison table reproduces the same series as 12 patients with 1-, 3- and 5-year overall survival of 75%, 54% and 42%. See the honest section.

alt.t: Where the local protocol is used, run the induction, restaging and adjuvant structure it specifies, and enter every patient in the prospective database.
alt.pref: Protocol candidates at this programme. The CPG requires platinum-based biliary chemotherapy or another standard regimen at the discretion of a protocol-approved oncologist; permits locoregional therapy other than external-beam radiation, but not as the sole pre-transplant therapy except for a solitary tumour under 3 cm; restages every three months; requires full explant histopathology with next-generation sequencing; sets tiered adjuvant therapy; and withdraws steroids rapidly with a view to mTOR-inhibitor conversion at four weeks.
alt.avoid: Do not treat the induction regimen list as current. It names FOLFOX, FOLFIRI, gemcitabine–capecitabine and gemcitabine–cisplatin and predates every immunotherapy combination now recommended; NCCN's current position for advanced mixed tumours is cisplatin–gemcitabine with either durvalumab or pembrolizumab. See Gate 7.
alt.note: The protocol's own adjuvant tiers have an internal gap: the moderate-risk tier requires a single lesion under 3 cm among its criteria, while the high-risk tier is triggered by a single lesion of 6 cm or more, so a single 4 cm well-differentiated tumour with clear margins and negative nodes falls into neither. Flagged for ratification. Its explant next-generation sequencing requirement is the right test ordered at the wrong time: in the largest genomic series, 34.7% of 150 cHCC-CCA carried a potentially actionable alteration, and a result that arrives on the explant cannot inform the induction regimen.

avoid.t: Do not list a patient on the strength of the words "regardless of size".
avoid.pref: Size is the variable on which the older and newer evidence agree. In the 19-patient multicentre transplant series, tumour size above 3 cm (p=0.038) and lymphatic invasion (p=0.023) were associated with mortality; recurrence occurred in 11 of 17 evaluable patients (64.7%) at a median of 4 months, and 1- and 3-year survival were 57.1% and 38.1% — with 95% confidence intervals of 0.301 to 1 and 0.137 to 1, which is to say those point estimates carry almost no information. The reason that series did so badly is in its baseline data: mean tumour 6.1 cm, 73.7% multinodular, 42.1% with vascular invasion, 36.8% beyond Milan, 10.5% with unsuspected nodal metastases, and 30-day mortality 10.5%.
avoid.avoid: The local CPG's 'regardless of size' is the single widest gap between it and every other document and every dataset: the OPTN pathway sets 3 cm, the ILTS-ILCA intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma statement sets 3 cm, the published series used Milan, and the UNOS analysis of 94 earlier recipients showed 1-, 3- and 5-year survival of 82%, 47% and 40%, similar to cholangiocarcinoma and significantly worse than HCC (86%, 72%, 62%, p=0.002). That UNOS cohort spans 1994 to 2013, records nothing about the tumour, coded only 6.3% as incidental — which the authors state is an undercount — and had recurrence data for just 27 of the 94, among whom 3-year recurrence was 93%. No Cox predictor in it reached significance, which with 94 patients means underpowered rather than absent.
avoid.note: The Spanish matched multicentre study is the one cohort here composed of knowingly abnormal nodules — incidental tumours were excluded by design — and in its 15 mixed HCC-CC patients 5-year survival was 78% against 86% in their matched HCC controls (p=0.9), with recurrence 7% against 4% (p=0.6). It is the most favourable comparison in the literature and it is 15 patients with a non-significant p value, matched on explant pathology that cannot be known at listing. Three exclusions matter: 8 patients beyond UCSF criteria, 16 patients who could not be matched because their disease was more advanced than any available HCC control, and whose 5-year survival was 28% with 51% recurrence, and the incidental cases. Even its uninodular subgroup of 2 cm or less, 12 per arm, showed 62% against 80% 5-year survival (p=0.4). The 27 pure iCCA patients in the same paper had 51% against 93% (p<0.001), so the pooled 42-patient figures should never be quoted.

avoid.t: Do not promise long-term graft and patient survival at HCC rates.
avoid.pref: Give the long-horizon numbers alongside the five-year ones. In the UNOS registry, 309 cHCC-CCA candidates had the lowest 3-year waitlist mortality (4.6%) and dropout (29.0%) of the three diagnoses compared — adjusted HR 0.33 (95% CI 0.12–0.89) for waitlist mortality and 0.56 (95% CI 0.36–0.86) for dropout — and the worst post-transplant outcomes: 5-year graft survival 58.7% (95% CI 52.2–64.6) and patient survival 60.3% (95% CI 53.7–66.2), falling to 37.6% and 40.3% at 10 years and 25.5% and 27.3% at 15 years, with adjusted hazard ratios of 1.79 (95% CI 1.50–2.13) for graft loss and 1.67 (95% CI 1.41–1.98) for death against HCC. Post-transplant recurrence was 23.0% against 11.3% for HCC (p<0.001) and came soonest in this diagnosis (2.7 ± 3.1 years).
avoid.avoid: A programme's own recent experience may be less favourable than the series it cites. In a matched single-centre cohort of 19 incidentally diagnosed cHCC-CCA recipients among 493 HCC transplants (3.9%), overall survival was 78.9% at 1 year and 23.8% at 3 and 5 years, and the excess hazard survived both matches: against controls matched on pre-transplant variables, overall survival HR 6.47 (95% CI 2.87–14.55) and recurrence-free survival HR 5.55 (95% CI 2.58–11.97); against controls matched on explant pathology, HR 4.67 (95% CI 2.07–10.53) and 3.65 (95% CI 1.70–7.82). Matching on what the explant showed does not explain the disadvantage away. Nine of the 19 died of metastatic adenocarcinoma, which names the cholangiocytic component as the cause of death. All 19 were assumed to be HCC before transplantation and received HCC-directed neoadjuvant treatment — this is the outcome of treating cHCC-CCA as HCC, not of a deliberate transplant decision.
avoid.note: The two findings are not contradictory, and the registry paper settles the question the single-centre series could not: it is the only analysis here with a waitlist denominator, and it shows cHCC-CCA candidates dropping out less often than either HCC or cholangiocarcinoma candidates. So the favourable per-protocol survival in the single-centre literature is not explained by dropout removing the patients who did badly. The deficit is after transplantation, not before it. Two cautions on the same paper: 250 of 278 transplanted patients (89.9%) carried a pre-transplant HCC diagnosis, so the cohort is a coding construct rather than a group known to have this disease at listing; and the reported improvement after MMaT-3 — 5-year graft survival 63.8% (95% CI 50.4–74.5) rising to 76.2% (95% CI 58.9–87.0) — has overlapping intervals, no test of interaction, shorter follow-up in the later era, and no selection data of any kind behind the authors' reading of it as refined selection.

avoid.t: Do not transplant for cHCC-CCA outside a written protocol with a registry, and do not let "the evidence now supports it" stand in for the sentence a consensus document actually wrote.
avoid.pref: Read the primary wording before quoting it. The 2024 ILTS-ILCA consensus makes no cHCC-CCA-specific statement at all: its only reference to the entity is that biopsy should be performed in HCC candidates to rule out cholangiocarcinoma or mixed tumours because they affect eligibility, prognosis and treatment. Its 3 cm statement is about intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma in cirrhosis (moderate evidence, moderate strength).
avoid.avoid: And the direction of the literature is not uniform. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 42 observational studies and 1,691 patients, all level 4 evidence, found median 5-year overall survival of 29% after hepatectomy against 41% after transplantation and recurrence of 65% against 54%, with no significant difference in the only 4 directly comparative studies (67 transplant against 227 resection patients) — and then concluded that hepatectomy should be preferred, which its own pooled estimates do not support. That paper is now eight years old and predates the 12-centre analysis, but the group should know that it exists, that it says the opposite, and that pooling single-arm proportions across 42 cohorts from different decades and classification eras does not produce a treatment effect either way.
avoid.note: Graft stewardship in a disease with 15-year patient survival of 27.3% against 45.9% for HCC is an institutional judgement, not an evidence question. It is approval item 1.

gates.name: 6 · The diagnosis arrived on the specimen
crit: A liver transplanted for presumed HCC whose explant shows a cholangiocytic component
A resection for presumed HCC or iCCA whose specimen shows both differentiations
A specimen in which the predominant component differs from the pre-operative biopsy
A margin, nodal, vascular or perineural finding that was not anticipated pre-operatively
gates.ask: The diagnosis changed after the operation — what changes now, and what does not?

standard.t: Treat the explant or resection specimen as the commonest route to this diagnosis, and build the pathway so that an unexpected result has a defined next step rather than a phone call.
standard.pref: Every programme. In the Korean single-centre transplant series, all 32 cHCC-CC cases were diagnosed incidentally in the explanted liver, 31 of 32 having been pre-diagnosed as HCC, and 12 of 32 (37.5%) had a separate concurrent HCC. In the 40-recipient Korean national registry series, none was identified before transplantation. In the French cirrhosis cohort, all 49 transplant diagnoses were made on the explant — 44 listed for HCC and 5 for decompensated cirrhosis. In the matched single-centre cohort, 19 of 19 were assumed to be HCC pre-transplant and all received HCC-directed neoadjuvant treatment.
standard.avoid: Do not treat the post-hoc diagnosis as a reason to re-litigate the transplant. It is a reason to re-stage, to intensify surveillance, and to decide adjuvant therapy with the explant variables in hand — and, at a programme level, to improve pre-operative detection.
standard.note: In the French multicentre cirrhosis series, incidental cHCC-CCA and iCCA of 5 cm or less in transplanted patients had 5-year survival of 69% at 2 cm or less and 65% above 2 cm, with no significant difference between the iCCA and cHCC-CCA patients (p=0.29) — and the two entities are not interchangeable, since the Spanish matched study put 5-year survival at 78% for mixed tumours against 51% for pure iCCA. The international 'very early' study is the clearest statement of how the explant defines these cohorts: 81 intrahepatic cholangiocarcinomas were found among 25,016 transplants at 17 centres, mixed HCC-CCA in the same nodule was excluded by design, 48 were analysed, and 46.7% of its favourable 15-patient group were incidental findings.

standard.t: Re-stage on the specimen with the AJCC intrahepatic bile duct categories, and report lymphovascular invasion, perineural invasion, tumour necrosis, component proportion and margin status explicitly.
standard.pref: Every specimen. These are the variables with the clearest outcome signal and none of them is in a radiological stage. Lymphovascular invasion separated 5-year overall survival of 93.3% from 35.8% in 80 hepatectomy patients, HR 11.35 (95% CI 3.20–40.3). Perineural invasion was present in 49 of 307 patients (16.0%) and carried worse median recurrence-free survival (0.21 against 0.54 years, HR 2.00, p<0.001) and overall survival (1.18 against 2.56 years, HR 2.21, p<0.001). Component proportion separated median overall survival of 3.16 years in HCC-dominant tumours from 1.86 years in CCA-dominant ones among 306 resections.
standard.avoid: Do not accept a report that gives only the two component names. The local CPG already requires complete explant histopathology plus next-generation sequencing, which is the right standard — the gap is that it asks for the sequencing on the explant rather than on the diagnostic specimen, by which point the result cannot inform induction therapy.
standard.note: Perineural invasion also had a direction effect that is worth knowing: the worst recurrence-free survival was in patients whose perineural invasion involved the HCC component, or was purely intratumoral. These are single-cohort subgroup findings from 307 patients, they have not been replicated, and that paper is one of the items on this page still cited from its abstract rather than from a full-text read. The transplant registry data agree on the variables while adding how thin they are: perineural invasion HR 5.14 (95% CI 1.07–24.69) on 4 patients and portal vein tumour thrombosis HR 13.43 (95% CI 2.17–83.21) on 3.

opts.name: Adjuvant systemic chemotherapy
opts.when: Two datasets point in different directions and neither is informative. In 75 patients after R0 resection at one centre, the 19 who received adjuvant chemotherapy had better overall survival on Kaplan-Meier (p=0.029) and after 1:2 propensity matching (p=0.0011), with the benefit confined to a nomogram-defined high-risk group (p=0.013; low-risk p=0.084) — a subgroup of 13 treated against 32 untreated patients, from a nomogram with a time-dependent AUC of 0.694 at two years. In 197 resected patients in SEER, median overall survival was 40 months (95% CI 26.4–53.7) without post-operative chemotherapy against 26 months (95% CI 18.6–33.4) with it, but the difference was not significant before matching (HR 1.290, 95% CI 0.850–1.956, p=0.20) or after it (HR 1.063, 95% CI 0.646–1.749, p=0.81).
opts.pref: A resected or transplanted patient with high-risk explant features — macrovascular invasion, nodal metastasis, a tumour above 5 cm, lymphovascular or perineural invasion, poor differentiation, or a positive margin — discussed as a shared decision with the numbers above stated.
opts.avoid: Do not present it as established, and do not present the SEER analysis as evidence against adjuvant therapy. Its chemotherapy arm had more advanced disease at baseline — T3–T4 in 25.5% against 15.2% (p=0.044), node-positive in 11.9% against 2.2% (p=0.003) — it excluded 87 transplant recipients, it records no recurrence and no second-line therapy, and its matched confidence interval still admits a 35% relative reduction in mortality. That is an uninformative null, not a negative result. The positive study is 19 treated patients whose own inclusion criteria excluded macrovascular invasion while the final model contains it. No adjuvant trial had ever enrolled this histology until 2025: patients with cHCC-CCA were systematically excluded from the landmark trials in both HCC and biliary tract cancer, so BILCAP, PRODIGE-12, BCAT and ASCOT say nothing about them.

opts.name: Post-operative adjuvant transarterial chemoembolisation
opts.when: The most consistently positive adjuvant signal in this disease, and the most clearly confined. In the 306-patient four-centre cohort, adjuvant TACE improved early recurrence-free survival only in HCC-dominant tumours (2-year early recurrence-free survival 53.3% against 32.3%, p=0.028) and not in balanced (p=0.276) or CCA-dominant (p=0.433) patients — and even there, overall recurrence-free and overall survival were both non-significant (p=0.068 and p=0.549) on 30 treated patients. In 95 radically resected patients, post-operative TACE was independently associated with better overall survival (HR 0.2, p=0.005) with no confidence interval reported. In 307 patients it improved early recurrence-free survival only in those without perineural invasion (p=0.031).
opts.pref: A resected, hepatitis-B-associated, HCC-dominant tumour at a centre that does this routinely, with the patient told the evidence is retrospective, confined to early recurrence, and almost entirely from one population.
opts.avoid: Not after transplantation, where the evidence does not exist at all and the risks differ. Not where perineural invasion is present, on the one dataset that examined the interaction. Not in a CCA-dominant tumour, where the only dataset that stratified by component found nothing. And note what happens when the same question is asked of a national registry: in the Taiwan Cancer Registry the hazard ratio for TACE was 0.56 in the non-surgical stratum and 1.64 in the surgical one — opposite directions in two strata of the same dataset, which is confounding by indication and not a treatment effect.

opts.name: Observation with intensive surveillance
opts.when: The honest default where no adjuvant modality has a trial behind it, and where the SEER analysis of post-operative chemotherapy could neither find nor exclude a benefit.
opts.pref: A low-risk explant — single tumour, well or moderately differentiated, no vascular, lymphovascular or perineural invasion, clear margins, negative nodes — and any patient whose recovery will not tolerate adjuvant treatment.
opts.avoid: Do not call it observation and then not observe. Surveillance intensity is the whole of this option's value and it has to be scheduled, not intended.

alt.order: The order is by strength of signal within an entirely retrospective literature, not by demonstrated benefit.
