There is no reported randomised evidence for any adjuvant strategy in cHCC-CCA, the two chemotherapy datasets are a 19-patient positive and a 59-patient uninformative null, and the TACE evidence is confined to early recurrence in HCC-dominant tumours in hepatitis-B-endemic populations and reverses direction between strata in a national registry.
alt.flagnote: Ratification item: does this programme offer adjuvant systemic therapy after resection or transplantation for cHCC-CCA, to whom, and with which regimen? The local CPG already specifies a post-transplant structure — six months total of neoadjuvant plus adjuvant therapy for a complete pathological response, three to six months for moderate-risk explants, and six months of a regimen different from the neoadjuvant one for high-risk explants — and none of that has comparative data behind it. It also leaves a gap: a single well-differentiated tumour between 3 and 6 cm with clear margins and negative nodes meets neither the moderate- nor the high-risk definition. There is now a prospective option to weigh against both: a single-arm phase II study of cadonilimab with capecitabine as adjuvant therapy after R0 resection of cHCC-CCA (NCT07243951, 75 patients planned, recurrence-free survival primary, powered against a historical median of 12.2 months). Audit: adjuvant modality, completion rate, and recurrence at two years by explant risk tier.

avoid.t: Do not start adjuvant capecitabine on BILCAP's authority, or any biliary adjuvant regimen on the assumption that this histology was in the trial.
avoid.pref: If adjuvant systemic therapy is given, give it as an explicit extrapolation, recorded as such, with the regimen chosen for the predominant component and the patient told there is no reported trial — and offer the trial that now exists. A single-arm phase II study of cadonilimab with capecitabine after R0 resection of cHCC-CCA opened in November 2025 (NCT07243951, 75 patients planned); it is the first adjuvant study in this histology, it compares against a historical control rather than a randomised arm, and it excludes patients with prior or planned liver transplantation.
avoid.avoid: cHCC-CCA has been systematically excluded from the landmark adjuvant trials in both HCC and cholangiocarcinoma. Quoting an adjuvant hazard ratio from a biliary trial to a patient with this histology misrepresents what is known.

avoid.t: Do not change immunosuppression on the explant finding alone without recording it as a decision with a reason.
avoid.pref: The local CPG's position — rapid steroid withdrawal, minimised immunosuppression, and consideration of conversion to an mTOR inhibitor at four weeks — is a reasonable one and is what the protocol says to do. Apply it as a protocol step, with the date and the reason in the note.
avoid.avoid: There are no comparative data on immunosuppression strategy after transplantation for cHCC-CCA specifically: the mTOR rationale is borrowed from HCC, and in the 40-recipient Korean registry series everolimus at 1, 6 or 12 months made no difference to survival or recurrence. An unrecorded change made on a pathology report is the kind of decision nobody can audit afterwards.

gates.name: 7 · Systemic therapy — which backbone, and why
crit: Unresectable, metastatic or recurrent disease, with no transplant pathway available or the patient declining it
A histological diagnosis, with the predominant component recorded where the specimen allows it
Multigene panel results in hand or requested
Performance status and hepatic reserve that will tolerate a platinum doublet
gates.ask: HCC backbone or biliary backbone — and on what am I basing that, other than habit?

opts.name: Cisplatin–gemcitabine plus durvalumab or pembrolizumab
opts.when: What NCCN names, and now the one option with a direct comparison behind it. Both the Hepatocellular Carcinoma and the Biliary Tract Cancers guidelines state that for histologically proven mixed tumours at advanced stages, cisplatin–gemcitabine with either durvalumab or pembrolizumab is an appropriate first-line choice, on the grounds that these combinations contain agents active in both histologies.
opts.pref: Most patients, and particularly a CCA-predominant tumour, a raised CA 19-9, or nodal and extrahepatic spread in a biliary pattern. In four Taiwanese centres, 21 patients with cHCC-CCA given first-line durvalumab with gemcitabine–cisplatin were compared with 154 patients with pure cholangiocarcinoma, all slides read jointly by two hepatopathologists: median overall survival 13.8 months (95% CI 2.1–25.6) against 13.3 months (95% CI 9.5–17.1), p=0.60, and after 2:1 propensity matching 13.8 against 14.5 months, p=0.78. Median progression-free survival was 5.3 against 5.1 months, objective response 38.1% against 23.8% after matching (p=0.24) with identical disease control at 66.7%, and histology was not an independent predictor of overall survival (HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.42–1.66). Grade 3 or worse toxicity was 57.1% against 42.9% after matching (p=0.30), with no immune-related adverse events in the cHCC-CCA patients and no treatment-related deaths.
opts.avoid: Read that comparison for what it is. Twenty-one patients with a confidence interval running from 2.1 to 25.6 months cannot demonstrate equivalence; a p value of 0.60 is a failure to detect a difference, and the hazard ratio admits both a 58% reduction and a 66% increase in mortality. Matching shrank the comparator from 154 to 42, so the matched analysis has 63 patients in total. No patient in it received an HCC regimen, so the comparison that would justify preferring a biliary backbone was never made — and the 21 were chosen for a biliary regimen by their own physicians, almost certainly on cholangiocarcinoma-like imaging or markers that the paper does not report. The older retrospective support is weaker still: in a 101-patient European cohort the 44 treated patients gave median overall survival of 15.5 months with chemotherapy against 5.3 months without, p=0.052 — not significant, not associated with survival on multivariable analysis, with objective response 8% against 5% and progression-free survival 3.0 against 3.2 months, and with 16 of the 19 non-chemotherapy patients on sorafenib. That is chemotherapy against sorafenib, and against a group too unwell for treatment at all.

opts.name: An HCC backbone — atezolizumab–bevacizumab, or tremelimumab–durvalumab
opts.when: Reasonable where the tumour is HCC-predominant, where AFP is the raised marker, and where cirrhosis limits chemotherapy tolerance. The genomic argument is real but narrower than it is usually stated: TP53 and TERT promoter alterations predominate and TERT promoter mutation is present in both components of the same tumour, establishing clonal common origin — but in 150 cHCC-CCA against 2,372 HCC, CTNNB1 was under 7% against over 34%, and the iCCA-typical drivers IDH1 (8.0% against 0.3%) and FGFR2 (7.3% against 0.3%) were present and are absent from HCC. This is not simply an HCC.
opts.pref: The HCC-predominant tumour in a cirrhotic patient, or a patient who cannot take a platinum doublet. In 16 patients given atezolizumab–bevacizumab across 7 French centres, the 9 treated in the first line had median overall survival 13 months, median progression-free survival 3 months and partial response in 3 of 9 (33%). In 21 Japanese patients given first-line HCC-directed therapy at 6 centres, objective response was 33.3% overall with disease control 95.2%, median overall survival 14.9 months (95% CI 9.7–19.3) and median progression-free survival 6.5 months (95% CI 4.9–10.8); by regimen, lenvatinib (n=14) gave 42.9% response and atezolizumab–bevacizumab (n=7) gave 14.3%.
opts.avoid: Severe gastrointestinal bleeding occurred in 2 of the 16 atezolizumab–bevacizumab patients (12.5%), which is a real signal in a cirrhotic population, and a 33% response rate from 3 responses in 9 patients has a confidence interval of roughly 7% to 70%. Note what the Japanese cohort is: median age 74, 19 of 21 ECOG 0, 18 of 21 Child-Pugh A, and 17 of 21 recurrences after prior local treatment — the fittest advanced population reported here — and no patient in it received a biliary regimen, so it cannot compare the two backbones either. IMbrave150 (HR for death 0.58, 95% CI 0.42–0.79) and HIMALAYA (median overall survival 16.43 against 13.77 months, HR 0.78, 96.02% CI 0.65–0.93) were trials in hepatocellular carcinoma and did not enrol this histology.

opts.name: Targeted therapy where an alteration is present
opts.when: NCCN states that at progression, molecularly targeted therapies should be considered where the tumour harbours a targetable aberration, and that panel testing should be considered in all advanced mixed tumours.
opts.pref: Any patient with an actionable result. In the largest genomic series, 52 of 150 cHCC-CCA (34.7%) carried a potentially actionable alteration against 462 of 2,372 HCC (19.5%), comprising IDH1 or IDH2 in 16, FGFR2 in 11, BRCA1 or BRCA2 in 7, ERBB2 in 5, BRAF in 4 and MET in 3. A separate 72-case series found FGFR2 alteration in 26.4% and HER2 immunohistochemistry 3+ in 8.3%, and a machine-learning classification of 73 tumours put potentially actionable alterations at 24.6%, concentrated in the CCA-like group where FGFR2, IDH1 and ARID1A each reached 25%.
opts.avoid: Do not expect the target frequencies of pure iCCA, and do not treat the 34.7% as a property of the disease: it rests on 52 patients in a commercial sequencing cohort selected by whose physician ordered profiling, and it bundles approved FGFR and IDH indications with MET and amplification targets that have no liver-cancer data at all. Do not test for mismatch-repair deficiency as the only molecular test — none was found in 24 cHCC-CCA in one series or in 72 in another, and only 2.7% of 150 were tumour-mutational-burden high. And every targeted agent in this setting is used on a basket or extrapolated indication, with no reported trial in this disease.

standard.order: The first option is first because NCCN names it and because it is now the only one with a direct comparison behind it — a 21-patient matched cohort in which cHCC-CCA did as well as pure cholangiocarcinoma on the TOPAZ-1 regimen. That is a failure to detect a difference in 21 patients, not a demonstration of equivalence, and no study compares an HCC backbone with a biliary backbone in this disease: no patient in either supporting cohort crossed over. The third option is third because it depends on a test result, not because it is weaker.
standard.flagnote: Ratification item: does this programme adopt NCCN's cisplatin–gemcitabine plus checkpoint inhibitor as the default first line for all advanced cHCC-CCA, or does it choose the backbone by predominant component, and if so on what threshold? The component proportion data — median overall survival 3.16 years for HCC-dominant against 1.86 years for CCA-dominant among 306 resected tumours — are prognostic, not predictive, and the one advanced-disease cohort that tested them found no difference between HCC-dominant and iCCA-dominant tumours at any threshold from 20% to 80%. Using them to pick a regimen is reasoning rather than evidence. The local CPG's induction list predates all of this and needs replacing. Registry: backbone chosen, predominant component, response, overall survival.

standard.t: Order multigene panel testing in every patient entering systemic therapy, and screen for trial eligibility at the same visit — there are now open trials in this histology, and the only one that ever randomised patients closed with four.
standard.pref: Every advanced case. No prospective trial in this disease has ever reported, so a trial is often the best available option and the panel result is what opens it. Four studies are currently open or about to open, all single-arm: durvalumab with a single priming dose of tremelimumab plus gemcitabine–cisplatin (NCT06855225, 29 patients, response rate primary, University of Alabama at Birmingham); hepatic arterial infusion chemotherapy with camrelizumab and rivoceranib (NCT07105748, TASK-05, 45 patients, recruiting in Shanghai); GEMOX with anlotinib and sintilimab (NCT06033118, 25 patients, Sichuan University, registry status last recorded as unknown); and the adjuvant study of cadonilimab with capecitabine after R0 resection (NCT07243951, 75 patients). A Japanese single-arm study of atezolizumab–bevacizumab in 12 patients (jRCTs031220099) is also reported. Reviews of the retrospective experience put gemcitabine–platinum median overall survival at 10.2–16.2 months with objective response 15–29%, and checkpoint-inhibitor objective response at 20–33%, with roughly 57% of tumours showing an immune-high phenotype and about a quarter carrying a targetable alteration.
standard.avoid: Do not wait for the explant to sequence, which is what the local CPG currently specifies — by then the result cannot inform induction. Do not read the immune-high figure as a predictive biomarker; it is a descriptive finding in 96 patients. And do not read those ranges as pooled estimates: the review that assembles them states plainly that they are the span of two or three cohorts of 7 to 101 patients, with no weighting and no confidence intervals, and that the molecular treatment algorithm it proposes is unvalidated for efficacy.
standard.note: The correction this page needed most in this gate is a factual one. It is not true that no prospective trial has ever existed: NCT05211323, a National Cancer Institute randomised phase II comparing gemcitabine–cisplatin–atezolizumab with and without bevacizumab in advanced cHCC-CCA, with progression-free survival as its primary endpoint, opened in December 2022 across 37 US sites against a planned enrolment of 88. It accrued 4 patients, is listed as active but not recruiting with a primary completion date of 20 January 2026, and has posted no results. The accurate statement is that no prospective trial in this disease has ever reported, and that the one randomised attempt failed on accrual — which is the single most important fact for anyone deciding whether to refer a patient to one of the four studies now open.

alt.t: Combining liver-directed treatment with immune and targeted therapy is a reasonable approach in liver-dominant unresectable disease, on real-world data only.
alt.pref: Liver-confined or liver-dominant unresectable disease with preserved function. In 51 patients screened from 242 at a single Chinese centre, all Child-Pugh A and ECOG 0–1, median overall survival was 17.8 months (95% CI 12.4–23.2) and median progression-free survival 8.9 months (95% CI 5.8–12.0), with objective response 41.2% by RECIST 1.1 and 56.9% by mRECIST, disease control 78.4%, and grade 3 or worse adverse events in 6 patients (11.8%).
alt.avoid: Those are the best numbers on this page and they come from a single-arm retrospective cohort of 51 patients selected from 242, with no comparator — and the 50 patients excluded because they received something other than this combination are precisely the control group it lacks. Eleven of the 51 (21.6%) were downstaged to resection and their median survival was not reached against 17.2 months for the rest (p=0.005), so they are carrying the headline figure. Two-year overall survival was 20.3% against a median of 17.8 months, so the curve falls away sharply. Seven different checkpoint inhibitors and four targeted agents were used across three interventional protocols, so no single regimen was evaluated. Primary disease did better than recurrent disease (median overall survival 21.4 against 11.4 months, p=0.011), and HCC-dominant and iCCA-dominant tumours did not differ in overall or progression-free survival (p=0.835 and p=0.553) at any HCC-component threshold from 20% to 80% — a useful negative finding for the backbone question. Baseline disease was advanced: median largest nodule 8.2 cm, 82.4% multinodular, 51.0% node-positive, 62.7% stage IV.
alt.note: Grade C on the strength of a single-arm cohort. Nothing here justifies preferring this over a guideline-named regimen outside a protocol or trial.

alt.t: Re-biopsy at progression where areas of response and progression are discordant, and switch to the regimen appropriate to the component that is progressing.
alt.pref: A patient still fit for further therapy whose imaging shows one lesion growing while others respond. NCCN recommends considering this, and states that if the recurrence biopsy suggests isolated recurrence of either the HCC or the CCA component, a systemic therapy option appropriate for that component is reasonable.
alt.avoid: Do not assume the recurrence carries the same mix as the primary, and do not assume a single-component recurrence biopsy means the other component has gone — the same sampling problem applies, with CK19 positive in 33% of biopsies against 84% of the matching specimens. No study has measured how often a recurrence biopsy in this disease changes the regimen or whether doing so helps.
alt.note: This is the one place where the two-component biology is used constructively rather than apologetically.

avoid.t: Do not choose a tyrosine kinase inhibitor alone as first line on the ground that the tumour is "mostly HCC".
avoid.pref: If an HCC backbone is chosen, choose a current one. The non-cytotoxic arm of the 101-patient European cohort was 16 sorafenib patients out of 19, with objective response 5%, median progression-free survival 3.2 months and median overall survival 5.3 months against 15.5 months for chemotherapy (p=0.052).
avoid.avoid: In a 123-patient single-institution experience, gemcitabine–platinum gave a disease control rate of 78.4% against 38.5% for gemcitabine–fluoropyrimidine (p=0.008), and sorafenib only 20% — but read the survival endpoint, because that paper's own overall survival comparison was flatly null: 11.5 months with gemcitabine–platinum against 11.7 months with gemcitabine–fluoropyrimidine, p=0.9686, with sorafenib at 9.6 months. A regimen that doubles disease control and changes survival by nothing is telling you that stable disease here is not durable benefit. Both cohorts are retrospective and neither tested a modern immunotherapy doublet.

avoid.t: Do not quote a trial effect size from biliary tract cancer or from hepatocellular carcinoma as if it applied at full strength here.
avoid.pref: Say which trial the regimen comes from and that this histology was not in it — and now say it as a fact about the protocols rather than an inference. KEYNOTE-966 (n=1,069, median overall survival 12.7 against 10.9 months, HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.72–0.95) admitted only intrahepatic or extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma or gallbladder cancer, and its exclusion criteria list 'mixed tumor histology' in those words. TOPAZ-1 (n=685, 12.8 against 11.5 months, HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.66–0.97) admitted only intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma and gallbladder cancer. ABC-02 (n=410, 11.7 against 8.1 months, HR 0.64, 95% CI 0.52–0.80) established the backbone.
avoid.avoid: So the extrapolation is documentable rather than assumed, and the page should say which way the documents point. One thing is unresolved: a 2026 review states that KEYNOTE-966 included 13 cHCC-CCA patients with no subgroup analysis, which cannot be reconciled with a protocol that excludes mixed tumour histology by name, and that review also states TOPAZ-1 enrolled none. Until that is settled, treat both effect sizes as untransferable. The regimen choice is defensible on the one matched cohort that exists in this histology; the trial effect size is not transferable, and quoting it as if it were is how a page like this misleads.

gates.name: 8 · Liver-directed therapy, entirely borrowed
crit: Liver-confined unresectable disease, or bridging or downstaging on a transplant pathway
A tumour with an arterialised component, where an embolic response is mechanistically plausible
Preserved liver function, a patent portal vein, and no extrahepatic disease driving the prognosis
Explicit acknowledgement that no trial of any liver-directed modality has been conducted in this disease
gates.ask: Am I treating this because the tumour is arterialised, or because it is in the liver and there is a catheter available?

standard.t: Record every liver-directed treatment in this disease as borrowed evidence, and expect lower response than in hepatocellular carcinoma.
standard.pref: Every case. The reviews that address this question directly reach the same conclusion: liver-directed methods — TACE, percutaneous ethanol injection, hepatic arterial infusion, radioembolisation and ablation — are less effective here than in HCC because of the cholangiocytic component's vascularity and desmoplasia, and transarterial chemoembolisation may be effective in unresectable disease particularly where the tumour is hypervascular. The one dataset that tested vascularity as a selection variable agrees: adjuvant TACE improved early recurrence-free survival only in the HCC-dominant third of 306 resected tumours (53.3% against 32.3% at two years, p=0.028) and not in balanced (p=0.276) or CCA-dominant (p=0.433) patients.
standard.avoid: Do not quote an HCC response rate, a BCLC stage-based algorithm, or an iCCA radioembolisation series as though either applied directly. There is no prospective trial of any liver-directed modality in cHCC-CCA, and the evidence base for this gate is review-level synthesis of HCC and iCCA experience plus small retrospective cohorts. Both interventional reviews are explicit that essentially all their quantitative material concerns cholangiocarcinoma, and neither distinguishes the hypervascular HCC-dominant tumour that might respond to an arterial therapy from the hypovascular CCA-dominant one that will not.
standard.note: Grade D is the honest grade for this whole gate. It is labelled Standard because liver-directed therapy is what gets done, and the page's job is to say what is known about it, not to pretend the modality is unevidenced and then recommend it silently.

standard.t: On a transplant pathway, locoregional therapy is the instrument that generates the six months of documented stability the exception requires — plan it as part of the listing strategy, not as treatment in parallel with it.
standard.pref: Every protocol candidate. The OPTN review-board criteria require six months from diagnosis or last treatment with the tumour remaining 3 cm or less, no new lesions and no extrahepatic disease, with imaging every three months; the ILTS-ILCA consensus frames bridging with neoadjuvant therapy as a way of identifying favourable tumour biology, with more than six months of stability or successful downstaging (low evidence, weak strength).
standard.avoid: Do not let the locoregional plan and the listing clock be owned by different people. And note what the consensus statement actually claims: that bridging helps identify favourable biology, not that it improves outcome.
standard.note: The local CPG permits locoregional therapy other than external-beam radiation — TACE, radiofrequency ablation, Y-90 — but states it should not be the sole pre-transplant therapy except for a solitary tumour under 3 cm. That is the one place where the local document is more conservative than it needs to be and more specific than the evidence; it is also the only written local rule on the subject, so it stands until the group changes it.

opts.name: Transarterial chemoembolisation
opts.when: The most used modality and the one with the most supporting data, though all of it is retrospective and the benefit is confined. Post-operative adjuvant TACE was independently associated with better overall survival (HR 0.2, p=0.005, no confidence interval reported) in 95 radically resected patients, and in 306 resections it improved early recurrence-free survival only in HCC-dominant tumours, with overall recurrence-free and overall survival both non-significant even there (p=0.068 and p=0.549).
opts.pref: A hypervascular, HCC-predominant, liver-confined tumour with preserved function, and bridging on a transplant pathway.
opts.avoid: Do not use it for a hypovascular, CCA-predominant tumour and expect a response — the quantitative imaging work in this disease shows that a large hypovascular component is what distinguishes cHCC-CCA from HCC in the first place, and the one cohort that stratified adjuvant TACE by component found no signal outside the HCC-dominant group. And in the Taiwan national registry the hazard ratio for TACE was 0.56 in the non-surgical stratum and 1.64 in the surgical one, which is confounding by indication rather than an effect.

opts.name: Transarterial radioembolisation
opts.when: Covered in both interventional reviews as an option extrapolated from HCC and iCCA experience, with no cHCC-CCA-specific data.
opts.pref: A larger liver-dominant tumour, or one in which the biliary component makes a bland or chemoembolic response unlikely, at a centre with the dosimetry expertise.
opts.avoid: There is no series in this histology to quote. Treat it as protocol or registry territory rather than routine.

opts.name: Thermal ablation
opts.when: Radiofrequency and microwave ablation appear in the interventional reviews, and the local CPG permits them as pre-transplant therapy. Ablation is the modality most defensible for a solitary small tumour.
opts.pref: A solitary tumour under 3 cm in a position that allows a margin, in a patient on a transplant pathway or unfit for resection.
opts.avoid: Obtain the biopsy before ablation, because the tissue opportunity closes with it — NCCN says so for HCC and the point is sharper here, where the transplant pathway requires biopsy-proven mixed histology. An ablated tumour with no tissue diagnosis cannot enter the exception pathway.

alt.order: Ordered by how much published experience each has in this disease, which for the second and third options is none and for the first is retrospective adjuvant data confined to HCC-dominant tumours. No comparative study exists, so the order carries no survival claim whatsoever and should not be read as one.
alt.flagnote: Ratification item: does this programme adopt the local CPG's rule that locoregional therapy may not be the sole pre-transplant therapy except for a solitary tumour under 3 cm, or does it align with the OPTN wording, which requires only locoregional or systemic therapy with six months of stability and sets no such restriction? These two documents disagree and the patient in the gap — a solitary 3 to 5 cm tumour treated with TACE alone and stable for six months — is a real one. Audit: modality, response, time to listing, dropout.

avoid.t: Do not use external-beam radiation as pre-transplant therapy under the local protocol.
avoid.pref: The local CPG excludes external-beam radiation from the locoregional options it permits before transplantation, and that is the local rule.
avoid.avoid: No data support the exclusion in this disease specifically, and no data support the alternative either. The perihilar protocol's experience of radiation-related vascular friability, gastroduodenal ulceration and ischaemic cholangiopathy is the likely origin of the restriction and is a reasonable analogy, but it is an analogy. If the group wants to permit radiotherapy here it needs to say so and record why.

avoid.t: Do not treat a liver-directed response as evidence that the diagnosis was something other than cHCC-CCA.
avoid.pref: A good embolic response tells you the arterialised component responded. It does not reclassify the tumour, it does not remove the cholangiocytic component, and it does not change the staging system, the nodal question or the surveillance interval.
avoid.avoid: This is a specific trap in a disease whose diagnosis is often provisional: a tumour that behaves like HCC on treatment invites the board to quietly revert to the HCC pathway. The histology, not the response, decides which page you are on.

gates.name: 9 · Surveillance, and what to do at recurrence
crit: A resected or transplanted patient under surveillance
A new liver lesion, a rising AFP, or a rising CA 19-9
Nodal recurrence at the porta hepatis or portal vein–vena cava region
An isolated recurrence that local re-treatment could address
gates.ask: Is this disease recurring, which component is recurring, and is any of it still treatable locally?

standard.t: Surveil at biliary rather than hepatocellular intensity — cross-sectional imaging of the liver and chest with AFP and CA 19-9 every three months for the first two years — because most recurrences happen inside that window.
standard.pref: Every resected and transplanted patient. Median recurrence-free survival was 7.27 months in a 95-patient multicentre radical-resection cohort and 5-year recurrence-free survival was 12.2% in a 19-patient single-centre series, against a 5-year overall survival of 44.7% in the same 19 patients — most of these patients recur, and recur early. The contemporary surgical review puts post-operative recurrence above 60%. In the 306-patient component-proportion cohort, extrahepatic or combined recurrence accounted for 26.9% of recurrences in HCC-dominant tumours, 37.2% in balanced and 50.5% in CCA-dominant ones (p=0.043), so the more biliary the tumour the more the surveillance has to look outside the liver.
standard.avoid: Do not run a six-monthly HCC surveillance schedule. Grade D: no study has tested a surveillance interval in this disease, and the three-monthly interval is reasoning from the recurrence timing plus concordance with the OPTN pathway's own three-monthly imaging requirement. It is an operating rule, not an evidence threshold.
standard.note: Include the porta hepatis deliberately in the reporting request. The lymph node was the second commonest site of first recurrence in the Japanese resection series, unlike HCC, and where nodal recurrence occurs it concentrates at the hepatic hilum (62.3%) and the portal vein–vena cava region (39.6%) — from 53 patients who had already recurred in nodes, of whom 11 had cHCC-CCA, so that is a map of where to look rather than a measure of how often.

standard.t: Biopsy a recurrence whose component mix could change the regimen.
standard.pref: Any recurrence in a patient still fit for systemic therapy, particularly where response is discordant across lesions. NCCN recommends considering repeat biopsy in metastatic or locally advanced recurrence after prior resection or local therapy, to establish the dominant histology — and treating an isolated single-component recurrence with the regimen for that component.
standard.avoid: Do not re-biopsy where the result cannot change the plan, and do not read a single-component recurrence biopsy as proof that only that component remains. The sampling problem of Gate 1 applies unchanged: CK19 was positive in 33% of pre-operative biopsies against 84% of the matching specimens. No study has measured biopsy performance at recurrence in this disease.

opts.name: Local re-treatment of an isolated recurrence
opts.when: Repeat hepatectomy and ablation are both reported in the review literature, and no study has compared local re-treatment with systemic therapy at recurrence in this disease. The nearest signal is from conversion rather than recurrence: in a 51-patient advanced cohort, the 11 downstaged to hepatic resection had a median overall survival not reached against 17.2 months for the rest (p=0.005), which is selection as much as surgery.
opts.pref: A solitary intrahepatic recurrence after a long disease-free interval in a fit patient with adequate remnant — which, given 5-year recurrence-free survival of 12.2% and a median recurrence-free survival measured in months, is an uncommon patient.
opts.avoid: Do not offer repeat local treatment for early multifocal recurrence or for nodal recurrence. Early recurrence in this disease is a statement about biology, and the recurrence-pattern data put the liver and the regional nodes as the two dominant sites.

opts.name: Systemic therapy at recurrence
opts.when: The default for multifocal, nodal or extrahepatic recurrence. This is Gate 7, with the component question re-asked on the recurrence biopsy rather than the primary.
opts.pref: Most recurrences. Recurrent disease does worse than primary disease on the only cohort that separated them — median overall survival 11.4 against 21.4 months, p=0.011 — so the conversation should start from that figure, not from the first-line figures.
opts.avoid: Do not carry over a first-line regimen that has already failed, and do not assume the backbone chosen for the primary is still the right one.

opts.name: Best supportive care
opts.when: The right answer in a patient with poor performance status, decompensated liver function or rapid multifocal progression, and the one this page is least likely to be opened for.
opts.pref: State it as a choice, early, and involve palliative care at the same visit rather than later. In 529 SEER patients the median overall survival was 8 months, and in the Taiwan Cancer Registry 5-year overall survival for this histology was 25.7% across 95,149 primary liver cancers — both whole-registry figures dominated by patients who were never resected, which is the point when the question is whether to treat at all.
opts.avoid: Do not reach it by default after three lines of borrowed therapy in a patient who was never going to tolerate them. And do not quote either registry's treatment hazard ratios in that conversation: the SEER paper reports the surgery hazard ratio as 4.94 in its abstract and 4.18 in its table, and the Taiwan registry's TACE hazard ratio reverses between its surgical and non-surgical strata.

alt.order: Ordered from the narrowest applicable option to the broadest, not by comparative evidence — none exists for recurrence management in this disease. The one quantitative anchor is that recurrent disease does substantially worse than primary disease.
alt.flagnote: Ratification item: what surveillance schedule does this programme adopt after resection and after transplantation for cHCC-CCA, and for how long? No guideline specifies one for this histology; NCCN says plainly for biliary tract cancer that there are no data to support a specific surveillance schedule. Audit: surveillance adherence, site of first recurrence, and interval from operation to recurrence.

avoid.t: Do not call a new nodule a recurrence of one component without tissue, and do not call a second primary a recurrence either.
avoid.pref: In the Korean transplant series, 12 of 32 patients (37.5%) had a concurrent separate HCC in the same explant. A new nodule in a cirrhotic remnant liver may be a new HCC rather than recurrent cHCC-CCA, and the two have different implications for what to offer.
avoid.avoid: The labelling matters for the registry as well as for the patient: outcome figures in this disease are already distorted by cohorts that mixed true mixed tumours with separate synchronous primaries, and the 2019 classification explicitly puts the double-cancer and collision types outside the entity.

quickref.title: WHO 2019 — what the diagnosis now means
quickref.intro: For the moment at the board when someone asks whether the old subtype on the report still exists.
rows: Core definition
One tumour containing unequivocal hepatocytic and cholangiocytic differentiation
How it is made
Routine haematoxylin and eosin morphology; immunostains supportive, not essential
Recognised
Classical cHCC-CCA, plus intermediate cell carcinoma, in which all cells express both hepatocyte and cholangiocyte features
Dropped
The stem-cell subtypes of the 2010 classification — typical, intermediate, cholangiolocellular
Reassigned
Cholangiolocarcinoma, formerly the cholangiolocellular subtype, is now a subtype of small-duct iCCA unless an unequivocal HCC component coexists
Not this disease
Two separate tumours, one HCC and one iCCA, in the same liver; the Allen double-cancer and combined types; the Goodman collision and fibrolamellar types
Proportion threshold
None set by WHO and none set by the 2018 consensus; 30% cholangiocytic derived by ROC on its own 72-case cohort (AUC 0.717), 70% borrowed from other tumour types as the split in a 306-patient cohort
How reproducible
Pathologist agreement with the reference cHCC-CCA diagnosis kappa 0.19, inter-observer agreement kappa 0.37, across 405 cases
Frequency

1% to 10% of primary liver tumours on pathological review (NCCN); 0.08 per 100,000 in men and 0.03 in women in SEER, with that paper's own abstract stating the reverse; 263 of 20,853 new primary liver cancers (1.3%) in the Japanese nationwide survey, of which only 39 were pathologically diagnosed
Transition rule for older data
None. No mapping is provided, so pre-2019 series cannot be re-expressed in the new terms
quickref.foot: The reclassification narrows the entity without any outcome analysis attached to it, so most of the imaging and outcome literature describes a broader group of tumours than the term now denotes and no series can be reclassified retrospectively — read any pre-2019 study with that in mind, and note that several papers here, including the 2025 Korean registry analysis, state outright that their patients were not classified by the 2019 criteria. Proportion carries prognostic weight even though no threshold is validated: in 306 resected tumours split at 70%, median recurrence-free survival was 1.02 years for HCC-dominant, 0.36 for balanced and 0.30 for CCA-dominant, with median overall survival 3.16, 1.93 and 1.86 years and 5-year overall survival 46.1%, 26.1% and 28.3% — but balanced and CCA-dominant did not differ from each other, so the real finding is binary. A deep-learning model reclassified 405 cHCC-CCA tumours as HCC-like or iCCA-like, and in the transplant subset the two groups had 5-year overall survival of 76.4% against 45.4%, HR 2.69 (95% CI 1.15–6.31) — a research finding, not a clinical tool, and one that means every pooled survival figure for this entity is an average over two diseases.

quickref.foot: Perihilar bile duct cancer, gallbladder cancer and hepatocellular carcinoma have separate staging, so this is a deliberate choice of system and not an interchangeable one. BCLC has no nodal category at all, which is why staging this disease as HCC loses the variable that most often changes what can be offered. Two qualifications from the full-text read: the sentence covering combined tumours was confirmed only from NCCN's reproduction of the AJCC tables and not from the manual itself, and no study has validated this staging system in this histology. What outcome data there are suggest the stage is a weak predictor here — in 40 transplant recipients neither Milan status nor tumour number nor maximum size predicted survival or recurrence, while perineural invasion, portal vein tumour thrombosis and microvascular invasion did, and in 80 hepatectomy patients lymphovascular invasion separated 5-year survival of 93.3% from 35.8%. Record the stage and the pathological variables separately rather than treating the stage as the prognosis.

quickref.title: Transplant criteria — four documents, four thresholds
quickref.intro: The most consequential page here: these four are not the same criteria, the one that governs the allocation request is the first, and none of them was derived in patients known to have this disease before transplant.
rows: OPTN NLRB transplant-oncology guidance

Biopsy-proven solitary iCCA or mixed HCC-iCCA 3 cm or less, cirrhosis, unresectable, locoregional or systemic therapy, 6 months of stability from diagnosis or last treatment, no new lesions, no extrahepatic disease. Score MMaT-3. Extension needs imaging every 3 months confirming 3 cm or less and no extrahepatic disease
2024 ILTS-ILCA consensus

No cHCC-CCA-specific statement. Its only mention: biopsy should be performed in HCC candidates to rule out CCA or mixed tumours, which can affect eligibility, prognosis and treatment (weak evidence, moderate strength). Its 3 cm statement is about iCCA in cirrhosis (moderate evidence, moderate strength)
Where the 3 cm came from

The 17-centre 'very early' iCCA study, which excluded mixed HCC-CCA in the same nodule by design. Its favourable group is 15 explant-defined patients (46.7% incidental) with 65% 5-year survival; the 3 cm extension rests on an intermediate subgroup of 6 patients with 61% 5-year survival
NCCN
No size limit stated. Patients whose tumour is limited in size by centre-specific criteria should be considered for evaluation at a transplant centre
Local CPG, 11 April 2022

No size limit — 'regardless of size'. Cirrhosis not required. Biopsy or cytology showing malignancy, not necessarily mixed histology. 6 months of stability on neoadjuvant and locoregional therapy. Transperitoneal biopsy 'minimized but not excluded'. High-risk features 'may be excluded'
Published series

Milan criteria, applied retrospectively by radiological burden at diagnosis, in the 12-centre analysis; 2 cm or less in the most favourable subgroups. Radiological Milan understages this tumour: 84.2% within Milan on imaging fell to 36.8% on explant in a 19-patient matched series (p=0.01)
Prospective protocols

None. No prospective transplant protocol admits cHCC-CCA; the phase 2 study of transplantation for early iCCA (NCT02878473) was terminated for low accrual, and the open adjuvant study in this histology excludes transplant recipients
quickref.foot: Outcome context, with the n stated each time because these are small numbers and with the denominator stated because it is usually the problem. Within Milan in the 12-centre retrospective analysis, 67 cHCC-CCA recipients had 5-year overall survival of 70.1% against 73.4% for 1,814 HCC recipients (p=0.806) with higher 5-year recurrence (23.1% against 11.5%, p<0.001), and 5-year disease-free survival of 70.3% against 33.6% after resection (p<0.001) while overall survival against resection was not significant (70.1% against 49.7%, p=0.078) — in a cohort where only 2 of 99 transplant recipients were knowingly transplanted with the diagnosis and 84 of 99 had been listed as HCC. The best-designed comparison runs the other way: 19 incidental recipients matched twice, on pre-transplant variables and again on explant pathology, carried mortality hazard ratios of 6.47 (95% CI 2.87–14.55) and 4.67 (95% CI 2.07–10.53) against matched HCC. In the UNOS registry, 309 candidates had 3-year waitlist mortality of 4.6% and dropout of 29.0% — the lowest of the three diagnoses compared, so dropout does not explain the favourable per-protocol figures — with 5-year graft and patient survival of 58.7% and 60.3% falling to 25.5% and 27.3% at 15 years, adjusted HR 1.79 for graft loss and 1.67 for death, and recurrence 23.0% against 11.3% for HCC. The updated meta-analysis of 6 retrospective comparative studies gives a pooled 5-year odds ratio of 0.55 (95% CI 0.38–0.81, p=0.002) favouring transplantation, with 1-year (0.67, 0.39–1.15) and 3-year (0.70, 0.42–1.17) estimates not significant — across arms whose mean tumour size was 2.19–2.57 cm against 2.7–6.26 cm, with one of six studies matched, and with leave-one-out analysis flipping the significance of both the 3- and 5-year estimates. An older systematic review of 42 level-4 studies and 1,691 patients found 5-year overall survival of 29% after hepatectomy against 41% after transplantation with null comparative studies, and concluded for hepatectomy. Every one of these is retrospective, most report tumours found only on the explant, and none is a comparison of treatments in exchangeable patients. Verify the current OPTN text before any listing decision.
