quickref.foot: The pattern across every row is the same: nothing here is sensitive enough to exclude the diagnosis, and only the biopsy is specific enough to confirm it — and the biopsy misses half. A biopsy reporting cHCC-CCA is almost certainly right; a biopsy reporting pure HCC in a tumour whose markers or imaging do not fit has told you very little, and the CK19 figures say why: the needle sees the hepatocellular component and misses the biliary one. The explant literature is the proof — in one transplant series all 32 cases, in another all 40, in another all 49 and in another all 19 were diagnosed only after the organ came out, and in the UNOS registry 89.9% of transplanted cHCC-CCA patients carried a pre-transplant HCC diagnosis. Every series in this table had pathological proof in every lesion and down-sampled HCC relative to true prevalence, so only sensitivity and specificity transfer; the lesions managed on imaging alone are absent from all of them. The operational consequence is in Gate 1: decide in advance what a single-component biopsy will change, because with 48% sensitivity the answer is usually nothing.

honest.t: Almost everything on this page is extrapolated, and the page's previous wording on trials was wrong. It is not true that no prospective trial in this disease has ever existed. The accurate statement is that none has ever reported.
honest.why: NCT05211323, a National Cancer Institute randomised phase II comparing gemcitabine–cisplatin–atezolizumab with and without bevacizumab in advanced cHCC-CCA, with progression-free survival as its primary endpoint and histological eligibility written to the 2019 WHO definition, opened in December 2022 across 37 US sites against a planned enrolment of 88. It accrued 4 patients. It is listed as active but not recruiting, with a primary completion date of 20 January 2026 and no posted results. Four studies are currently open or about to open, all single-arm: durvalumab with a priming dose of tremelimumab plus gemcitabine–cisplatin (NCT06855225, 29 patients); hepatic arterial infusion chemotherapy with camrelizumab and rivoceranib (NCT07105748, 45 patients, recruiting); GEMOX with anlotinib and sintilimab (NCT06033118, 25 patients, registry status last recorded as unknown); and adjuvant cadonilimab with capecitabine after R0 resection (NCT07243951, 75 patients). No prospective transplant protocol admits this histology at all — the phase 2 study of transplantation for early intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma was terminated for low accrual, and the open adjuvant study excludes patients with prior or planned transplantation. So the right thing to tell a patient is that a trial exists for the first time, that the only randomised attempt failed on accrual, and that every number quoted to them comes from retrospective series.

honest.t: The exclusion of this histology from the trials whose regimens the page recommends is documentable, not assumed.
honest.why: KEYNOTE-966 admitted only intrahepatic or extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma or gallbladder cancer, and its exclusion criteria list 'mixed tumor histology' in those words. TOPAZ-1 admitted only intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma and gallbladder cancer. The HCC trials on this page — IMbrave150 and HIMALAYA — were trials in hepatocellular carcinoma. One thing is unresolved and should not be smoothed over: a 2026 review states that KEYNOTE-966 included 13 cHCC-CCA patients with no subgroup analysis, which cannot be reconciled with a protocol that excludes mixed tumour histology by name. Until that is settled, treat both effect sizes as untransferable in either direction.

honest.t: The paper that licenses transplantation for this disease cannot license a decision to list it. In the 12-centre analysis, only 11 of 208 patients had a pre-operative diagnosis of cHCC-CCA and only 2 of those 11 were transplanted; 84 of the 99 transplant recipients had been pre-diagnosed as HCC.
honest.why: The within-Milan survival equivalence that is quoted everywhere rests on 67 patients and a p value of 0.806 — a failure to detect a difference in a small subgroup, not a demonstration of equivalence. The significant finding in that same subgroup is the one that is rarely quoted: 5-year recurrence was 23.1% against 11.5% for HCC recipients, p<0.001, double the rate. Within Milan, transplantation beat resection on disease-free survival (70.3% against 33.6%, p<0.001) but not on overall survival (70.1% against 49.7%, p=0.078). Beyond UCSF criteria 5-year survival was 15.8%. There was no central pathology review across 12 centres over 9 years, in an entity where pathologist agreement is kappa 0.19 to 0.37, and there is no waitlist denominator, so patients listed as HCC who dropped out and were never found to have a mixed tumour are structurally invisible. The page keeps the recommendation and has downgraded it to D: there is no cohort of any size describing patients deliberately listed with this diagnosis.

honest.t: Imaging-based Milan classification systematically understages this tumour, which undermines the measurement every favourable transplant figure is built on.
honest.why: In 19 transplant recipients whose explants showed cHCC-CCA, 84.2% were within Milan on pre-transplant imaging but only 36.8% remained within Milan on explant pathology (p=0.01 against matched controls). The 12-centre analysis classified Milan status on initial imaging. Imaging-based classification is prospectively knowable, which is a genuine strength of that study, but it also means its 70.1% within-Milan survival describes a group that was substantially beyond Milan in reality, and the paper does not report how many. Any local rule that turns on radiological Milan should be written knowing that this disease will cross it silently in roughly half of patients.

honest.t: The 3 cm threshold that will decide your patient's exception request was derived in a population from which this histology was excluded.
honest.why: The OPTN transplant-oncology criteria and the ILTS-ILCA 3 cm statement trace to the 17-centre 'very early' intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma study, which made mixed hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma in the same nodule an explicit exclusion criterion — it is an iCCA series, and citing it in support of transplanting cHCC-CCA misreads its population. Its favourable group is 15 patients defined on explant pathology, of whom 46.7% were incidental findings, with 65% 5-year survival; the extension from 2 cm to 3 cm rests on an intermediate subgroup of 6 patients with 61% 5-year survival; central pathology review covered 67.9% of cases; and there is no waitlist denominator. The threshold is the one that governs the submission, so the page applies it. It is grade D however firmly a guideline states it.

honest.t: Waitlist dropout does not explain the favourable per-protocol figures. The deficit in this disease is after transplantation, not before it.
honest.why: This is the one thing the 2026 UNOS analysis settles, and it is the only paper here with a waitlist denominator. Among 66,889 adults listed for a primary liver cancer, the 309 cHCC-CCA candidates had the lowest 3-year waitlist mortality (4.6%, adjusted HR 0.33, 95% CI 0.12–0.89) and the lowest dropout (29.0%, adjusted HR 0.56, 95% CI 0.36–0.86) of the three diagnoses compared. So the usual defence of the single-centre literature — that the good survival figures are an artefact of the sickest candidates falling off the list — does not hold. What follows is worse, not better: 5-year graft and patient survival of 58.7% and 60.3%, falling to 25.5% and 27.3% at 15 years, with adjusted hazard ratios of 1.79 for graft loss and 1.67 for death against HCC, recurrence 23.0% against 11.3%, and the shortest time to recurrence of the three diagnoses. Two cautions on the same paper: 89.9% of the transplanted patients carried a pre-transplant HCC diagnosis, so the cohort is a coding construct rather than a group known to have this disease at listing, and the post-MMaT-3 improvement the authors highlight has overlapping confidence intervals, shorter follow-up and no selection data behind it.

honest.t: The programme's own most recent published experience points the other way from the paper its protocol rests on, and it is now the better-designed study.
honest.why: The 2018 propensity-matched analysis of 12 recipients concluded that low-grade cHCC-CCA should not be excluded from transplantation. The 2026 matched cohort of 19 incidentally diagnosed recipients among 493 HCC transplants matched twice — once on pre-transplant variables and once on explant pathology — and found mortality hazard ratios of 6.47 (95% CI 2.87–14.55) and 4.67 (95% CI 2.07–10.53), with recurrence-free survival hazard ratios of 5.55 and 3.65. Matching on what the explant showed does not explain the disadvantage away, which is what makes that design informative. Nine of the 19 died of metastatic adenocarcinoma, naming the cholangiocytic component as the cause of death, and overall survival was 23.8% at 3 and 5 years. Both studies are small, single-centre, retrospective and from the same institutional lineage, and they disagree. This remains the most important thing for a human to adjudicate on this page — but the evidence has moved, and it has moved against the permissive reading.

honest.t: The 2018 propensity-matched series on which the local protocol rests was not obtained for this revision, and the page no longer cites it as read.
honest.why: Its figures here come from the 2026 transplant overview's secondary report of it and from a 2026 comparison table: 5-year recurrence-free survival 42% against 44% when matched on explant pathology (p=0.45), but 28% against 61% when matched on pre-transplant characteristics (p=0.12), in 12 patients with 1-, 3- and 5-year overall survival of 75%, 54% and 42%. The direction of that asymmetry is the argument — matched on what is knowable before transplant, the mixed-tumour patients did worse — and it runs with the 2026 double-matched cohort, not against it. A previous version of this page quoted a within-series breakdown of recurrences by differentiation grade from that paper; it could not be verified from any source obtained and has been removed.

honest.t: Differentiation grade is the right selection criterion measured at the wrong time, and the page's grade for it has been downgraded accordingly.
honest.why: The evidence that pathology predicts recurrence is reasonably consistent: poor differentiation was independently predictive of recurrence in the French cirrhosis cohort (HR 4.16, 95% CI 1.37–12.66) in a 45-patient subgroup model, and in the 40-recipient Korean registry series microvascular invasion predicted recurrence-free survival (HR 4.56, 95% CI 1.36–15.22) while perineural invasion (HR 5.14, on 4 patients) and portal vein tumour thrombosis (HR 13.43, on 3 patients) predicted survival. Every one of those is an explant finding. In that registry cohort no pre-operative variable — not Milan status, not tumour number, not maximum size — predicted anything at all. Pre-transplant grading of a two-component tumour on a needle core is unreliable, the core may sample only one component, and no study has tested whether biopsy grade predicts explant grade in this disease. The local CPG's softening of poor differentiation from a criterion that 'must' exclude to one that 'may' exclude is therefore a decision taken without the evidence either way — and the right response is to find a pre-operative surrogate and audit it, not to argue about the wording.

honest.t: The entity may be two diseases, and if it is, every pooled survival figure on this page is a weighted average of them in unknown proportions.
honest.why: A deep-learning model trained on HCC and iCCA slides reclassified 405 cHCC-CCA tumours as HCC-like or iCCA-like, and in the liver transplant subset the two groups had 5-year overall survival of 76.4% against 45.4%, HR 2.69 (95% CI 1.15–6.31). Component proportion does something similar on routine pathology: 5-year overall survival 46.1% in HCC-dominant tumours against 26.1% and 28.3% in balanced and CCA-dominant ones among 306 resections. Neither split is usable prospectively — both are measured on a resection or an explant — and the model has no ground truth, having been validated against a reference standard the same paper shows to be unreliable at kappa 0.19 to 0.37. But a 31-percentage-point difference in post-transplant survival inside the entity means that two series reporting different survival may simply contain different mixtures, and that the right question at the board is which component is driving this tumour rather than what the literature says about the average one.

honest.t: The diagnosis is usually made after the decision it should have informed, and the full-text read quantifies why the needle cannot fix that.
honest.why: In one transplant series all 32 cases were found incidentally in the explanted liver; in the Korean national registry all 40; in the French cirrhosis cohort all 49, where a known cholangiocarcinoma diagnosis was an absolute contraindication; in a matched single-centre cohort all 19, who were assumed to be HCC and given HCC-directed neoadjuvant treatment; and in the UNOS registry 89.9% of transplanted patients carried a pre-transplant HCC diagnosis. The mechanism is sampling, and it has a number: CK19 was positive in 33% of pre-operative biopsies against 84% of the matching surgical specimens. Biopsy alone is 48% sensitive at 100% specificity, imaging and biopsy together reach 60%, and in the 19-patient multicentre series 4 patients were biopsied and all 4 were read as HCC. Nor is pathology self-correcting: when 117 cases called HCC that carried iCCA-typical alterations were re-reviewed, the HCC diagnosis was confirmed in only 48 (41%). This is not a failure of local practice — it is the natural history of a diagnosis that requires two differentiations in one tumour and a needle that samples a few millimetres of it.

honest.t: No imaging test on this page can exclude the diagnosis, and the one that matters most for a transplant programme has never been measured.
honest.why: At least one LR-M feature was present in 93.9% of cHCC-CCA but also in 51.5% of HCC, so specificity is 48.5%; a three-feature rule reaches 80.8% accuracy at 54.5% sensitivity; targetoid appearance alone was present in 75.8% of cHCC-CCA and 65.2% of matched HCC. On contrast-enhanced ultrasound the CEUS LI-RADS criteria for cHCC-CCA were 40.0% sensitive with an AUC of 0.649, and the authors honestly recalculated the positive predictive value at real prevalence as 1.6% to 39.6%. LI-RADS protects the HCC diagnosis rather than finding this one: LR-5 was 89–90% specific but cHCC-CCA made up 63–86% of the false-positive LR-5 reads, and LR-M with LR-TIV caught only 62–71% of cHCC-CCA against about 90% of iCCA. The best marker-plus-MRI model published separates cHCC-CCA from mass-forming iCCA with an AUC of 0.807 — and that study had no HCC comparator group at all, so the error that puts a mixed tumour onto an HCC transplant pathway remains unquantified. Every one of these series had pathological proof in every lesion and down-sampled HCC relative to true prevalence, so the lesions managed on imaging alone are absent from all of them.

honest.t: The local Mixed Hepatocholangiocarcinoma CPG's diagnostic criterion cannot be met as written. It asks for "imaging characteristics consistent with intrahepatic mixed hepato-cholangiocarcinoma on CT or MRI" plus biopsy or cytology showing malignancy.
honest.why: No such imaging phenotype exists — that is the finding of every imaging study in the disease — and a biopsy showing malignancy is a criterion for cancer, not for this cancer. The OPTN review-board pathway that now governs the exception request requires biopsy-proven mixed HCC-iCCA. A patient can satisfy the local document completely and have no evidence of cholangiocytic differentiation at all. This is the single wording on the local protocol most likely to produce a declined request, and it is an easy fix.

honest.t: The local CPG's "regardless of size" is the widest gap between any two documents on this page, and the evidence does not support it.
honest.why: The OPTN pathway sets solitary and 3 cm or less; the ILTS-ILCA iCCA statement sets 3 cm; the 12-centre series used Milan; the most favourable subgroups in the Spanish and Korean series were 2 cm or less. Size above 3 cm was associated with mortality in the 19-patient multicentre transplant series, whose mean tumour was 6.1 cm with 73.7% multinodular disease and 36.8% beyond Milan, and which recurred in 64.7% at a median of 4 months. In the Spanish matched cohort even the uninodular tumours of 2 cm or less gave 62% against 80% 5-year survival (12 per arm, p=0.4), and 16 patients were removed from that study because their disease was too advanced to match any HCC control — those 16 had 28% 5-year survival and 51% recurrence. The CPG was written when there was no exception pathway to align with; there is one now. Two further gaps sit alongside it. The CPG's adjuvant risk tiers contradict themselves — the moderate-risk tier requires a single lesion under 3 cm while the high-risk tier is triggered at 6 cm or more, so a single 4 cm well-differentiated tumour with clear margins and negative nodes meets neither definition. And its induction regimen list (FOLFOX, FOLFIRI, gemcitabine-capecitabine, gemcitabine-cisplatin) predates TOPAZ-1, KEYNOTE-966, IMbrave150 and HIMALAYA, where NCCN's current position for advanced mixed tumours is cisplatin-gemcitabine with durvalumab or pembrolizumab. The document's newest reference is from 2018 and it cites NCCN v1.2017.

honest.t: Regional lymphadenectomy is recommended here on staging logic and recurrence pattern, not on a demonstrated survival benefit — and the cohort usually cited against it contradicts its own title.
honest.why: No study has shown that nodal dissection improves survival in cHCC-CCA. The case for it is that nodal status is an AJCC category that cannot be recovered later, that the lymph node is the second commonest site of first recurrence in this tumour where it is not in HCC, that the narrative surgical literature puts nodal metastasis at 25–35%, and that the guideline governing the staging system carries out a porta hepatis dissection. The 179-patient cohort that reports selective dissection as safe found no adjusted difference in overall survival (HR 0.78, 95% CI 0.46–1.30) but a significantly worse adjusted progression-free survival without dissection (HR 2.12, 95% CI 1.20–3.77, p=0.012). Its undissected group survived longer because it was more favourable: 54% of them were cHCC-CCA against 19% of the dissected, with smaller and earlier tumours and CA 19-9 missing in 70%. Only 26% of its dissections reached 6 nodes, and its cHCC-CCA subgroup analyses, on 77 patients, were all non-significant. The nodal mapping study that defines where to dissect had 11 cHCC-CCA patients among 53 and counts recurrences rather than patients at risk.

honest.t: Choosing between an HCC backbone and a biliary backbone is still reasoning rather than evidence, but the terms of the argument have changed in both directions.
honest.why: For the biliary backbone there is now one direct comparison: 21 patients with cHCC-CCA given first-line durvalumab with gemcitabine–cisplatin had median overall survival of 13.8 months against 13.3 months in 154 patients with pure cholangiocarcinoma, 13.8 against 14.5 after matching, with histology not an independent predictor (HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.42–1.66). That is an underpowered null — the confidence interval for the cHCC-CCA group runs from 2.1 to 25.6 months — and no patient in it received an HCC regimen, so the comparison that would justify the conclusion was never made. Against the biliary backbone, the retrospective support previously quoted on this page does not hold up: the 101-patient European cohort's 15.5 against 5.3 months was p=0.052, lost significance on multivariable analysis, and compared chemotherapy with sorafenib and with no treatment at all; and the 123-patient series that established gemcitabine–platinum did so on disease control (78.4% against 38.5%, p=0.008) while its overall survival comparison was flatly null (11.5 against 11.7 months, p=0.9686). For the HCC backbone, the genomic argument needs restating: TP53 and TERT promoter alterations do predominate and clonal common origin is established, but in 150 cHCC-CCA against 2,372 HCC, CTNNB1 was under 7% against over 34%, while IDH1 (8.0% against 0.3%) and FGFR2 (7.3% against 0.3%) were present and are essentially absent from HCC. This is not simply an HCC, and the 20-tumour series that found no IDH1, IDH2, FGFR2 or BAP1 at all could not have excluded those frequencies. Component proportion remains prognostic and not predictive: the one advanced-disease cohort that tested it found no survival difference between HCC-dominant and iCCA-dominant tumours treated identically at any threshold from 20% to 80%.

honest.t: The adjuvant question is open, and neither of the two datasets usually set against each other is informative.
honest.why: In 75 patients after R0 resection, the 19 given adjuvant chemotherapy had better overall survival unmatched (p=0.029) and after matching (p=0.0011), with benefit confined to a nomogram-defined high-risk group — 13 treated against 32 untreated patients, from a nomogram with a time-dependent AUC of 0.694, in a study whose inclusion criteria excluded macrovascular invasion while its final model contains it. In 197 resected SEER patients, median overall survival was 40 months without chemotherapy and 26 months with it, but the difference was not significant before matching (HR 1.290, 95% CI 0.850–1.956) or after it (HR 1.063, 95% CI 0.646–1.749); the treated arm had more T3–T4 disease (25.5% against 15.2%) and four times the node positivity (11.9% against 2.2%); 87 transplant recipients were excluded; and no recurrence data exist. The matched interval still admits a 35% relative mortality reduction. That is an uninformative null, not evidence against adjuvant therapy, and the page previously read it the wrong way. Adjuvant TACE has the most consistent signal and the narrowest one: benefit confined to early recurrence-free survival in HCC-dominant tumours (53.3% against 32.3% at two years, p=0.028, on 30 treated patients), with overall recurrence-free and overall survival non-significant even there, and with the Taiwan registry's TACE hazard ratio reversing between strata (0.56 non-surgical, 1.64 surgical). The first prospective adjuvant study in this histology (NCT07243951) is single-arm against a historical control.

honest.t: Liver-directed therapy in this disease has no trial, no series of any size, and no modality comparison. Its entire evidence base is review-level synthesis of HCC and iCCA experience.
honest.why: Both interventional reviews state that essentially all their quantitative material concerns cholangiocarcinoma, and neither distinguishes the hypervascular HCC-dominant tumour that might respond to an arterial therapy from the hypovascular CCA-dominant one that will not — which is the single most important selection variable in this gate. The one dataset that stratified by component found adjuvant TACE helped only HCC-dominant tumours and only for early recurrence. The strongest number anywhere in this area is adjuvant post-operative TACE in 95 resected patients (HR 0.2 for overall survival, p=0.005, no confidence interval reported), from a hepatitis-B-endemic population, retrospective, with adjuvant TACE almost certainly given to selected patients. The page labels this Standard because it is what gets done and the board needs the honest figures, not because the modality is evidenced.

honest.t: Two intervals on this page are operating rules rather than evidence thresholds: the local protocol's three-monthly MR bone survey, and the three-monthly surveillance schedule this page recommends after treatment.
honest.why: The MR bone survey appears in no guideline and has no supporting data in this disease. It is a plausible safeguard in a tumour that metastasises to bone and it is the local written rule, so it stands until the group changes it — but it is grade D, it runs three times per listing cycle, and nobody has measured what it finds. The post-treatment surveillance interval is derived from recurrence timing: median recurrence-free survival of 7.27 months in a 95-patient resection cohort, 5-year recurrence-free survival of 12.2% in another, and recurrence above 60% in the narrative literature, so most events fall inside the window. No study has tested a surveillance interval in this histology, and NCCN states plainly for biliary tract cancer that there are no data supporting a specific schedule or set of tests. That the interval also matches the OPTN pathway's own imaging requirement is convenient, not evidential.

honest.t: Several of the registry papers this page relies on contain internal numerical contradictions, and their affected figures should not be quoted at a board.
honest.why: The SEER population study reports the higher incidence in women in its abstract while its text and table give 0.08 per 100,000 in men against 0.03 in women, and reports the hazard ratio for surgery as 4.94 in the abstract and 4.18 in the table. The Korean registry analysis reports 3-year overall survival by MELD in a direction opposite to its own Cox model, figure risk table and conclusion, and reports a single-tumour subgroup as 18 patients where its figure legend and risk table indicate about 7. The Taiwan registry's TACE hazard ratio reverses between its surgical and non-surgical strata. In each case the descriptive survival figures remain usable and the treatment or subgroup estimates do not. More broadly, nine of the sources on this page are still cited from their abstracts rather than from a full-text read, and two papers in the depot could not be obtained at all — see the provenance note for which.

honest.t: A number of figures that appeared on the previous version of this page could not be verified against the full text and have been removed rather than softened.
honest.why: They included a 5-year cause-specific survival of 17.7% and a 39.5% resection rate attributed to the SEER population study; a denominator of 100,754 liver cancers and a set of mortality percentages attributed to the Taiwan registry, where the study reports 95,149 cancers and 5-year overall survival of 25.7%; a 21-of-27 resection rate and comparator survivals of 33% and 37% attributed to the first Western series, which reports a 24% 5-year survival after resection in a cohort with no cirrhosis; 1- and 3-year survival percentages and a multinodular comparison attributed to the Spanish matched cohort, which reports 5-year survival of 78% against 86% (p=0.9) in 15 patients; recurrence-site counts attributed to the 80-patient Korean hepatectomy series; recurrence-biopsy counts attributed to the 19-patient Japanese resection series; a contrast-enhanced ultrasound paper cited in support of FDG-PET; and a '1,321-transplant single-centre series' with 24 explant diagnoses attributed to the international very-early iCCA study, which reports 81 explant cholangiocarcinomas among 25,016 transplants at 17 centres. Where a verified figure exists it has replaced the unverified one; where none exists the claim has gone. A reader comparing the two versions should know that the removals are a correction, not a change of position.

honest.t: This page has no ratified roadmap behind it and no institutional position to report, so where the documents disagree it shows the disagreement rather than resolving it.
honest.why: The five existing disease pages transcribe a Memorial Hermann system roadmap that already exists and has been through specialty review. This one does not. Its only local source is a five-page transplant clinical practice guideline approved on 11 April 2022, which is authoritative for the transplant gate and silent on everything else — diagnosis outside the transplant context, staging, resection, lymphadenectomy, systemic therapy for non-candidates, liver-directed therapy, surveillance. Every one of those gates on this page is a draft written from guidelines and primary literature, and every flagnote is a decision the group has not yet taken.

board: Submission — an Epic form captures the imaging category and the specific LR-M features present, AFP and CA 19-9 with their dates, cirrhosis status and aetiology, whether tissue has been obtained and by what route, the histology including component proportion if known, nodal and extrahepatic findings, prior treatment, and whether the question is diagnosis, resectability, transplant candidacy or systemic therapy. Owner: submitting clinician.

Triage — a coordinator and a clinically trained gatekeeper check completeness, imaging adequacy and currency, whether histology exists, and whether the case is really a cHCC-CCA case or a separate synchronous HCC and iCCA, which is a different problem. Owners: coordinator and chair.

The diagnosis flag — any case submitted as HCC with a raised CA 19-9 or CEA, or with any LR-M feature, is tagged at triage so the mixed question is asked explicitly rather than discovered on the specimen. This is the single highest-yield operational step in this disease. Owner: coordinator.

Attendance — hepatobiliary and transplant surgery, hepatology, medical oncology, diagnostic radiology, interventional radiology, radiation oncology and pathology are all required. A transplant surgeon must be present for any cirrhotic patient with a tumour of 3 cm or less, whatever the submitted question, because the needle and the operation can both close that door. Owners: specialty leads.

Pathology — pre-alerted for every case where cHCC-CCA is the question, so that both differentiations are looked for and the report states the component proportion, differentiation grade, lymphovascular and perineural invasion, margin status and nodes retrieved and involved. A biopsy originally read as HCC or iCCA in a flagged case is re-reviewed. Owner: pathology.

Radiology — the observation is categorised with the LI-RADS version stated, the individual LR-M features are listed rather than summarised, and the porta hepatis and portal vein–vena cava nodal stations are reported explicitly on every study. Owner: diagnostic radiology.

Staging statement — every case leaves the board with an AJCC 8th edition intrahepatic bile duct stage recorded, or an explicit note that it cannot yet be assigned and why. A BCLC stage alone is not an acceptable output. Owner: chair.

The transplant criteria line — where transplantation is discussed, the note records which document the plan is being measured against: the OPTN review-board criteria, the local CPG, or Milan as used in the published series. Naming the document is the point, because they differ — and the note records that radiological Milan understages this tumour, 84.2% within Milan on imaging having fallen to 36.8% on explant in the one series that measured both. Owner: transplant surgery.

Output — one recommendation, one owner, one due date, one reassessment date, one documented alternative considered, and a statement of what the histology is currently believed to be and on what evidence. Owner: chair.

Trial screening — every advanced case and every resected case is screened against the open studies in this histology at the board at which it is first discussed, and the result is recorded. The only randomised trial ever opened in this disease closed with 4 patients, which is what happens without a standing rule. Owner: medical oncology.
Documentation — an Epic note within one business day in the agreed structured format, naming any claim that rests on extrapolation from HCC or from iCCA. Owner: named owner.

Registry — every case closed in the registry with the pre-operative histology, the specimen histology, the imaging category, the biopsy route, the decision, the modality delivered and the outcome at reassessment. In a disease this rare the registry is the only way the programme will ever have its own numbers. Owner: coordinator.

Referring relationships — the referring clinician is told the recommendation, who owns the next step, and specifically if the histology has changed from what they referred, since it changes surveillance in their hands. The pathway returns patients with a plan; it does not capture them. Owner: named owner.
dashboard: Pre-operative histology against specimen histology, every case — the detection rate is the programme's core quality metric in this disease (approval item 3).
Proportion of cases submitted as HCC in which a raised CA 19-9 or CEA, or an LR-M feature, was present and not acted on before operation or listing.
Biopsy rate and route in cirrhotic patients with a tumour of 3 cm or less, and whether a transplant surgeon reviewed the case before the needle (approval item 2).
Nodes retrieved and nodes involved at every hepatectomy, stratified by pre-operative diagnosis, with nodal recurrence at two years (approval item 4).
Resection outcomes: R0 rate, 90-day mortality, median and 5-year recurrence-free and overall survival, with lymphovascular and perineural invasion recorded.

Transplant pathway: patients entered, dropout and reason, time from diagnosis to listing, exception requests submitted and granted or declined with the reason, and the criteria document each was measured against (approval items 1 and 5).
Milan or OPTN status assigned on imaging at listing against the explant tumour burden, every recipient, with the discordance rate (approval item 11).
Second pathology read: proportion of flagged cases reviewed by a second pathologist, and the rate at which the diagnosis changed (approval item 12).

Post-transplant recurrence and graft and patient survival for every cHCC-CCA recipient, including those diagnosed only on explant, reported against the programme's own matched HCC recipients rather than against the literature (approval item 1).
Systemic therapy: backbone chosen, predominant component, multigene panel result and whether it changed the regimen, objective response, progression-free and overall survival (approval item 6).
Adjuvant therapy after resection and after transplantation: modality, risk tier assigned, completion rate, and recurrence at two years (approval item 7).
Liver-directed therapy: modality, indication (definitive, bridging, downstaging or adjuvant), radiological response, and time to progression (approval item 8).
Surveillance adherence against the three-monthly schedule for the first two years, with site of first recurrence and interval from operation (approval item 9).
Registry closure rate: proportion of cHCC-CCA cases with complete pre-operative and specimen histology, decision and outcome recorded.
Trial screening and referral: advanced and resected cases screened for eligibility, referrals made, enrolments (approval item 13).
Pre-transplant biopsy grade against explant grade, every recipient, as a concordance rate (approval item 14).

approvals.q: Does this programme transplant for combined hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma, under whose governance, and against which written criteria?
approvals.why: The evidence is entirely retrospective and the two most relevant single-centre series from this institutional lineage point in opposite directions — a 2018 propensity-matched analysis of 12 recipients argued that low-grade tumours should not be excluded, and a 2026 matched cohort of 19 incidentally diagnosed recipients found mortality hazard ratios of 6.47 (95% CI 2.87–14.55) against controls matched on pre-transplant variables and 4.67 (95% CI 2.07–10.53) against controls matched on explant pathology. The multicentre licence is thinner than it looks: in the 12-centre analysis only 2 of 99 transplant recipients were knowingly transplanted with the diagnosis, the within-Milan equivalence is a p value of 0.806 in 67 patients, and recurrence in that same subgroup was double (23.1% against 11.5%, p<0.001). UNOS data show the lowest waitlist mortality and dropout of the three diagnoses compared and the lowest 15-year graft and patient survival, so dropout does not explain the favourable per-protocol figures. Graft stewardship at 27.3% 15-year patient survival is an institutional judgement, not an evidence question.
approvals.audit: Registry mandatory if the pathway stays open: every recipient including explant-diagnosed cases, with recurrence, graft and patient survival, reported against the programme's own matched HCC recipients.

approvals.q: Is the local Mixed Hepatocholangiocarcinoma CPG of 11 April 2022 reaffirmed, revised, or replaced?
approvals.why: Its diagnostic criterion cannot be met as written — there is no cHCC-CCA imaging phenotype, and it asks only for biopsy or cytology showing malignancy where the OPTN pathway requires biopsy-proven mixed histology. It permits listing 'regardless of size' where every other document and every dataset sets a limit. It does not require cirrhosis. It states that the MELD exception will be sought 'once the exception is available from UNOS', and it is now available and narrower than the protocol. Its induction regimen list predates every immunotherapy combination now recommended, it specifies next-generation sequencing on the explant rather than the diagnostic specimen when 34.7% of these tumours carry a potentially actionable alteration, its adjuvant tiers leave a 3-to-6 cm gap, and its newest reference is from 2018.
approvals.audit: Named owner, a revision date, and a standing reconciliation against the current OPTN guidance text and NCCN editions.

approvals.q: What triggers the cHCC-CCA question in a patient submitted as hepatocellular carcinoma — and is a biopsy then mandatory?
approvals.why: This is where the disease is won or lost. NCCN already names raised CA 19-9 or CEA with suspicion of iCCA or cHCC-CCA as an indication for core needle biopsy even in a lesion meeting HCC imaging criteria, and the ILTS-ILCA consensus recommends biopsy in HCC candidates to rule out a mixed tumour. Against that, biopsy has its own costs and most of these diagnoses are still made on the specimen. The group has to decide whether the NCCN footnote becomes a local rule.
approvals.audit: Pre-operative histology against specimen histology, every case; and the proportion of flagged cases in which the trigger was acted on.

approvals.q: Routine porta hepatis lymphadenectomy for every resection in which cHCC-CCA is known or suspected, or a selective policy with a documented reason?
approvals.why: No study shows a survival benefit for lymphadenectomy in this disease. The case for routine dissection is that nodal status is an AJCC category that cannot be recovered later, the lymph node is the second commonest site of first recurrence here but not in HCC, nodal metastasis is reported in 25–35% of cHCC-CCA, and the iCCA guideline that governs the staging system carries out a porta hepatis dissection. The case against is morbidity in a cirrhotic liver and a 179-patient cohort in which selective dissection showed no adjusted difference in overall survival (HR 0.78, 95% CI 0.46–1.30) — but that same cohort found adjusted progression-free survival significantly worse without dissection (HR 2.12, 95% CI 1.20–3.77), only 30% of patients had any dissection and only 26% of those reached 6 nodes, the indication was confounded by the pre-operative label (OR 3.33), and its 77-patient cHCC-CCA subgroup analyses were all non-significant.
approvals.audit: Nodes retrieved and involved by pre-operative diagnosis, with nodal recurrence at two years.

approvals.q: Which size threshold does the programme apply for transplant candidacy: the OPTN 3 cm solitary limit, Milan as used in the published series, or something else?
approvals.why: These are different thresholds and they will select different patients. The local protocol's 'regardless of size' is not supported by any dataset. Referral and allocation are also distinct — NCCN sets no size limit for referral and leaves it to centre criteria, while the exception request will be judged at 3 cm. A patient can be reasonably referred, reasonably transplanted under a local protocol, and still fail the exception.
approvals.audit: Exception requests submitted, granted or declined with the reason, and the criteria document each was measured against.

approvals.q: Default first-line backbone for advanced disease — NCCN's cisplatin–gemcitabine plus a checkpoint inhibitor for everyone, or backbone chosen by predominant component?
approvals.why: There is now one direct comparison and it is an underpowered null: 21 patients given first-line durvalumab with gemcitabine–cisplatin had median overall survival of 13.8 months (95% CI 2.1–25.6) against 13.3 months in 154 patients with pure cholangiocarcinoma, 13.8 against 14.5 after matching, with histology not an independent predictor (HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.42–1.66) — and no patient in it received an HCC regimen. The older retrospective support is weaker than the page previously implied: the European cohort's 15.5 against 5.3 months was p=0.052 and non-significant on multivariable analysis against a mostly sorafenib comparator, and the series that established gemcitabine–platinum did so on disease control while its survival comparison was null (11.5 against 11.7 months, p=0.9686). The genomic data no longer point cleanly the other way either: CTNNB1 is under 7% against over 34% in HCC, while IDH1 and FGFR2 are present at 8.0% and 7.3% and absent from HCC. The one cohort that compared HCC-dominant with iCCA-dominant tumours treated identically found no difference at any threshold from 20% to 80%. Component proportion is prognostic, not predictive.
approvals.audit: Registry: backbone chosen, predominant component, panel result, response, progression-free and overall survival.

approvals.q: Adjuvant therapy after resection and after transplantation — to whom, which modality, and for how long?
approvals.why: The two retrospective datasets on adjuvant chemotherapy are a 19-patient positive and an uninformative null: benefit after propensity matching in 75 patients at one centre, confined to a nomogram-defined high-risk subgroup of 13 treated patients from a model with an AUC of 0.694; and in 197 SEER patients a numerically worse median survival with chemotherapy that was not significant before matching (HR 1.290, 95% CI 0.850–1.956) or after it (HR 1.063, 95% CI 0.646–1.749), in a treated arm with more T3–T4 disease and four times the node positivity. Post-operative TACE has the most consistent signal but only for early recurrence and only in HCC-dominant tumours (53.3% against 32.3% at two years, p=0.028, on 30 patients), and the Taiwan registry's TACE hazard ratio reverses between strata. The first prospective adjuvant study in this histology is now open (NCT07243951, single-arm, 75 patients). The local protocol's post-transplant tiers are unevidenced and leave a 3-to-6 cm gap in their own definitions.
approvals.audit: Adjuvant modality, risk tier assigned, completion rate, recurrence at two years by tier.

approvals.q: Does locoregional therapy alone qualify a patient for the transplant pathway, and may external-beam radiation be used?
approvals.why: The local CPG says locoregional therapy must not be the sole pre-transplant therapy except for a solitary tumour under 3 cm, and excludes external-beam radiation. The OPTN wording requires only locoregional or systemic therapy with six months of stability and imposes neither restriction. The patient in the gap — a solitary 3 to 5 cm tumour treated with TACE alone and stable for six months — is a real one, and the two documents give different answers.
approvals.audit: Modality, indication, response, time to listing, and dropout.

approvals.q: Surveillance schedule after resection and after transplantation, and for how long?
approvals.why: No guideline specifies one for this histology, and NCCN says plainly for biliary tract cancer that there are no data to support a specific schedule or set of tests. The three-monthly interval on this page is derived from recurrence timing — median recurrence-free survival of 7.27 months in one resection cohort, 5-year recurrence-free survival of 12.2% in another — and from the OPTN pathway's own imaging requirement, not from a comparative study. The one variable that should shape it is the component proportion: extrahepatic or combined recurrence rose from 26.9% in HCC-dominant tumours to 50.5% in CCA-dominant ones (p=0.043).
approvals.audit: Surveillance adherence, site of first recurrence, interval from operation to recurrence.

approvals.q: Does this draft become the programme's pathway for this disease, and who owns it?
approvals.why: Unlike the five existing disease pages, this one has no ratified roadmap behind it. The only local source is a transplant clinical practice guideline that is authoritative for one gate and silent on the other nine. Every gate outside the transplant question is a first draft written from guidelines and primary literature, and it needs specialty review before it is treated as institutional policy.
approvals.audit: Named owner, version and date, a multidisciplinary approval record, and an agreed update cycle covering NCCN editions, OPTN guidance revisions and the WHO classification.

approvals.q: Does the programme accept radiological Milan as a listing criterion in this disease, knowing that it understages it?
approvals.why: In 19 transplant recipients with explant cHCC-CCA, 84.2% were within Milan on pre-transplant imaging and only 36.8% on explant pathology (p=0.01). The 12-centre analysis that supplies the favourable within-Milan survival classified burden on initial imaging, so that figure describes a group substantially beyond Milan in reality. The group has to decide whether it applies a stricter radiological limit than Milan for this histology, whether it uses the OPTN 3 cm solitary limit as the operative rule throughout, and what it does with a patient whose explant crosses a criterion the imaging said they met.
approvals.audit: Imaging-based Milan or OPTN status at listing against explant tumour burden, for every recipient, with the discordance rate reported annually.

approvals.q: What pathology safeguard does the programme adopt, given that the diagnosis is reproduced at kappa 0.19 to 0.37?
approvals.why: Pathologist agreement with the reference cHCC-CCA diagnosis was kappa 0.19 across 405 cases, with inter-observer agreement kappa 0.37. When 117 cases called HCC that carried iCCA-typical alterations were re-reviewed, the HCC diagnosis was confirmed in only 41%. Biopsy is 48% sensitive and CK19 is positive in 33% of biopsies against 84% of the matching specimens. The question is whether every flagged case gets a second reader, whether any case gets external or central review, and whether a genomic result that does not fit the histology triggers a re-read.
approvals.audit: Proportion of flagged cases with a documented second pathology read, and the rate at which the diagnosis changed on re-review.

approvals.q: What is the programme's trial policy in this disease, now that trials exist?
approvals.why: The page can no longer say that no prospective trial has ever existed. Four studies are open or about to open — NCT06855225, NCT07105748, NCT06033118 and the adjuvant NCT07243951 — and the only randomised attempt, the NCI's NCT05211323, closed accrual at 4 patients against a planned 88. That failure is the strongest argument for a standing referral rule rather than case-by-case recall: a disease at roughly 0.5% of liver cancer transplant listings will not accrue to a trial unless every case is screened. The group has to decide whether to screen every advanced case, whether to seek participation in a study, and who owns the screening.
approvals.audit: Proportion of advanced and resected cases screened for trial eligibility, referrals made, and enrolments.

approvals.q: May a needle-biopsy differentiation grade exclude a transplant candidate, when no study has tested biopsy grade against explant grade in this disease?
approvals.why: Grade and the other pathological variables carry the most reproducible outcome signal — poor differentiation HR 4.16 (95% CI 1.37–12.66) for recurrence in the French cirrhosis cohort, microvascular invasion HR 4.56 (95% CI 1.36–15.22) in the Korean registry — and all of them are explant findings. In that registry cohort no pre-operative variable predicted anything. The local CPG softened these from criteria that 'must' exclude to features that 'may' exclude. The group has to decide whether a needle-core grade is allowed to make an exclusion, or whether the criterion is recorded as unmeasurable before transplant and the decision made on size, number, nodal status and observed stability instead.
approvals.audit: Pre-transplant biopsy grade against explant grade for every recipient, reported as a concordance rate.

nccnhcc: National Comprehensive Cancer Network. Hepatocellular Carcinoma. NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology. Programme-supplied extraction; the Discussion section is dated 14 August 2026 and references are accessed to 2 April 2026, but the extraction carries no printed version number, so the edition must be confirmed before the page is used as policy. Sections relied on: Principles of Mixed HCC-CCA (resection as standard for resectable disease; evaluation at a transplant centre where the tumour is limited in size by centre-specific criteria; repeat biopsy at recurrence; cisplatin-gemcitabine plus durvalumab or pembrolizumab first line; multigene panel testing); Principles of Core Needle Biopsy (raised CA 19-9 or CEA with suspicion of iCCA or cHCC-CCA as a biopsy indication, and referral to a transplant centre before biopsy in a potential candidate); Principles of Pathology (reporting non-hepatocellular components).
nccnbtc: National Comprehensive Cancer Network. Biliary Tract Cancers. NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology. Version 1.2026, 10 March 2026 (Discussion section last updated 2 July 2025). Sections relied on: Principles of Mixed HCC-CCA, which is substantively identical to the HCC guideline's page and adds that multigene panel testing should be considered in all advanced mixed tumours; Principles of Surgery for intrahepatic disease (regional lymphadenectomy of the porta hepatis; nodal disease beyond the porta hepatis and distant metastasis contraindicate resection; pre-operative biopsy not always necessary; minimally invasive approaches in well-selected cases); AJCC 8th edition intrahepatic bile duct TNM Tables 5 and 6 with the regional node definition; and the statement that there are no data supporting a specific surveillance schedule.
optnnlrb: Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network, Liver and Intestinal Organ Transplantation Committee. Guidance to Liver Transplant Programs and the National Liver Review Board for: Adult MELD Exceptions for Transplant Oncology. Retrieved 6 October 2026; the document carries no printed version or approval line, and a copy also circulates dated February 2025, so the current text must be confirmed before any listing decision. Its Intrahepatic Cholangiocarcinoma section is the only policy-side document that names this disease: biopsy-proven unresectable solitary iCCA or mixed hepatocellular carcinoma/intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma 3 cm or less, with cirrhosis, after locoregional or systemic therapy, with 6 months from diagnosis or last treatment of stability meaning 3 cm or less, no new lesions and no extrahepatic disease; exception score MMaT-3; extension requires imaging every 3 months confirming 3 cm or less and no extrahepatic disease; submitted by selecting Cholangiocarcinoma on the form. Whether this is a standardised exception under OPTN Policy 9.5.A or a review-board determination was not established for this draft and must be checked against the current policy text.
who2019: WHO Classification of Tumours Editorial Board. Digestive System Tumours. WHO Classification of Tumours, 5th edition, volume 1. Lyon: International Agency for Research on Cancer; 2019. The source of the definition this page uses — a single tumour with unequivocal hepatocytic and cholangiocytic differentiation, diagnosed on routine morphology — of the retention of classical cHCC-CCA and intermediate cell carcinoma, of the removal of the stem-cell subtypes of the 2010 edition, of the reassignment of cholangiolocarcinoma to small-duct intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, and of the exclusion of the Allen double-cancer and combined types and the Goodman collision and fibrolamellar types. The primary volume was not in hand for this draft; the content above is taken from the editorial board's own published summary of the fifth edition (PMID 31433515), read in full on 7 October 2026, together with the consensus and review literature that reports it (PMIDs 29360137, 33545267, 32729276, 39936601). It should still be checked against the volume before publication. Note that the reclassification carries no outcome analysis and provides no mapping rule, so pre-2019 series cannot be re-expressed in its terms.
ajcc8: Amin MB, Edge SB, Greene FL, et al, editors. AJCC Cancer Staging Manual. 8th edition. Chicago: American Joint Committee on Cancer / Springer; 2017. Liver and intrahepatic bile ducts. The staging system this page applies, on the manual's own statement that all intrahepatic bile duct carcinomas, including combined hepatocellular cholangiocarcinomas, are covered by it. T, N, M and stage-group definitions as reproduced in NCCN Biliary Tract Cancers v1.2026 Tables 5 and 6; the manual itself was not in hand and the wording covering combined tumours was confirmed from a secondary source, so verify it directly before publication.
localcpg: Mixed Hepatocholangiocarcinoma (HCC-CCA) Clinical Practice Guideline. Liver Transplant Program; five pages; approved by the Liver CMPI Subcommittee 11 April 2022. Revision history: initial draft 27 April 2018 (Dr Keri Lunsford), initial approval 9 July 2018 by the Liver CMPI Subcommittee with Dr Ghobrial's revisions changing 'must' to 'should' and to 'may be excluded', revision 20 March 2022 (Dr Sudha Kodali) to read 'mixed hepato-cholangiocarcinoma', approved 11 April 2022. The authority for Gate 5 and for the induction, restaging, explant, adjuvant and immunosuppression structure on this page. Its newest cited reference is from 2018 and it cites NCCN Hepatobiliary Cancers v1.2017; the 2022 revision was a change of terminology, not of content, and it therefore predates the WHO 2019 reclassification, the 12-centre transplant analysis, the 2024 ILTS-ILCA consensus and the OPTN transplant-oncology guidance that now covers this diagnosis.
roadmapnone: Unlike the five existing disease pages (hepatocellular carcinoma, colorectal liver metastases, intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, perihilar cholangiocarcinoma and neuroendocrine liver metastases), combined hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma has no Memorial Hermann system roadmap and no guideline alignment worksheet. provenance: Second pass, revised 7 October 2026 after a full-text read of the page's primary literature. Every paper in the depot — 52 of them — was read in full and abstracted to a structured record carrying the authors' own stated limitations and an independent critique, and this page was then reworked gate by gate against those records. The revision corrected numbers, added the halves of results that had been left out, downgraded items whose critique undercut the claim, and removed figures that could not be verified; the honest section grew from 12 items to 22 and is the most useful part of the page. Three papers were added: the WHO editorial board's own summary of the 2019 classification (PMID 31433515), the first real-world comparison of the TOPAZ-1 regimen in cHCC-CCA against pure cholangiocarcinoma (PMID 42413329), and the largest genomic series in the entity, 150 cHCC-CCA against 2,372 HCC (PMID 41564818). The trial registry was read directly on 7 October 2026 to correct this page's previous claim that no prospective trial had ever existed: one randomised phase II did exist, accrued 4 patients of a planned 88 and has never reported, and four single-arm studies are now open or about to open. What is still cited from an abstract rather than a full-text read, and should be checked before any figure from it is used at a board: Beaufrère 2021 (33545267), the 2024 ILTS-ILCA consensus (40014003), the multicentre perineural invasion study (40675210), and the five trials quoted for their effect sizes — TOPAZ-1 (38319896), KEYNOTE-966 (37075781), ABC-02 (20375404), IMbrave150 (32402160) and HIMALAYA (38319892). Two papers could not be obtained at all: the 2018 propensity-matched transplant series (29573187), whose figures appear here only as reported by Lee 2026 and by the comparison table of Kodali 2026 and which is not cited as read, and Campani 2026 (41865801), which is not cited on this page. The AJCC manual and the WHO volume were likewise not in hand; the AJCC tables are as reproduced in NCCN and the WHO content is from the editorial board's summary and the consensus literature. There is no ratified Memorial Hermann system roadmap for combined hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma and no guideline alignment worksheet, so this page states no institutional position outside the transplant gate and resolves no guideline disagreement on its own authority. The one local source is the Mixed Hepatocholangiocarcinoma (HCC-CCA) Clinical Practice Guideline of the Liver Transplant Program, approved by the Liver CMPI Subcommittee on 11 April 2022 (initial draft 27 April 2018, approved 9 July 2018, revised 20 March 2022); it is the authority for Gate 5 and for the induction, restaging, explant, adjuvant and immunosuppression structure, and it is silent on diagnosis outside the transplant context, staging, resection, lymphadenectomy, systemic therapy for non-candidates, liver-directed therapy and surveillance. Its newest reference is from 2018, it cites NCCN Hepatobiliary Cancers v1.2017, and its 2022 revision changed terminology rather than content, so the page flags where it has fallen behind: the WHO 2019 reclassification and the definitional requirement for one tumour with two differentiations; the OPTN National Liver Review Board transplant-oncology guidance, which now provides the MELD exception the CPG says is awaited, at a narrower threshold of biopsy-proven solitary mixed HCC-iCCA of 3 cm or less with cirrhosis against the CPG's 'regardless of size'; the requirement for biopsy-proven mixed histology rather than cytology showing malignancy; the softening of poor differentiation to a feature that 'may be excluded'; an induction regimen list that predates every immunotherapy combination now recommended; a 3-to-6 cm gap in its own adjuvant risk tiers; and next-generation sequencing specified on the explant rather than the diagnostic specimen. The guideline sources are the programme-supplied NCCN extractions — Hepatocellular Carcinoma, Principles of Mixed HCC-CCA, Principles of Core Needle Biopsy and Principles of Pathology, whose Discussion is dated 14 August 2026 but which carries no printed version number in the extraction, and Biliary Tract Cancers v1.2026 of 10 March 2026, Principles of Mixed HCC-CCA, Principles of Surgery for intrahepatic disease and the AJCC 8th edition intrahepatic bile duct tables — together with the OPTN transplant-oncology guidance as retrieved on 6 October 2026, the 2024 ILTS-ILCA consensus (which makes no cHCC-CCA-specific statement), and WHO Digestive System Tumours 5th edition 2019 as reported in the editorial board's summary and the consensus and review literature rather than from the volume itself. The primary literature is 61 papers, every PMID verified against PubMed on 6 October 2026. Every treatment claim on this page is retrospective or extrapolated: no prospective trial in this disease has ever reported, patients with this histology were excluded from the landmark trials in both hepatocellular carcinoma and biliary tract cancer — by name in the case of KEYNOTE-966 — and so no item on the page is graded above C and most of the operating rules are D. This page is a draft for multidisciplinary review, it is not active clinical policy, it does not replace clinician judgement, and every numeric criterion — the OPTN text above all — must be verified against the current source before use.
